title: Security brief - Thursday 19 November 2026

top.headline: Java4Shell: critical OpenJDK flaw fixed, scanning and exploit attempts reported but no confirmed compromise
top.summary: Oracle and the OpenJDK project fixed CVE-2026-114938 on 17 Nov. The finder, Calif, reports unauthenticated remote code execution in six enterprise products; other labs reproduced memory corruption and crashes. CISA and CERTs in Canada, the EU, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands and New Zealand issued alerts; GreyNoise, watchTowr and Cloudflare report probing, and several vendors say they know of no malicious use.
top.label: CONFIRMED

top.headline: Optimizely platform hijacked to serve malicious code on 178 organisations’ websites
top.summary: On 16 Nov an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation sign-up flow to inject malicious JavaScript, which Report URI found in 188 snippets across 178 organisations including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, GitLab and IKEA. Optimizely confirms the incident and says it closed the flaw and cleaned affected projects; its start time differs from Report URI's by about three and a half hours.
top.label: CONFIRMED

top.headline: Run of US outages: officials and companies say no cyber link; root causes largely unpublished
top.summary: Microsoft (M365, 12 Nov), the FAA (ground stop, 13 Nov), the NSA's classified network and Apple's iCloud (both 17 Nov) each suffered outages. Each organisation points to internal causes, and US officials told Congress on 18 Nov they have no indication the incidents are linked or malicious; the theory that AI-driven patching contributed remains unproven and is disputed.
top.label: CONFIRMED

items.headline: Run of US tech outages: Apple cites 'internal update' for ~6-hour iCloud disruption; officials see no cyber link, AI-patching theory contested
items.summary: Apple's 17 Nov outage (iCloud sign-in, AppleCare, App Store, Apple Business) was attributed by Apple to an internal update, not a cyberattack, while US officials told Congress on 18 Nov they have no indication that the week's outages (Microsoft, FAA, United, JPMorgan, Marriott, NSA) are linked or malicious; claims that AI or AI-driven patching played a role remain unproven.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.firstReported: 17 Nov 16:15 UK (AppleInsider, citing Apple's status page: AppleCare on Device, all users); wave began 12 Nov

sections.happened:
**Wave (US dates; UK is GMT, 5 hours ahead of ET):**

- Thu 12 Nov: Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams outage. Microsoft attributed it to a latent defect from a July gateway-server update plus load and reduced gateway capacity (Cybernews; The Next Web, citing Microsoft's preliminary report).
- Fri 13 Nov: FAA nationwide ground stop of more than four hours (AP). Officials said FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris had performed maintenance at a remote facility; the FAA and L3Harris are still investigating the root cause (CBS; CNBC).
- Mon 16 Nov: United Airlines system outage lasted more than 90 minutes and delayed departures (AP via PBS). JPMorgan Chase reported a temporary issue linked to a software bug in on-premises hardware systems (AP; Cybernews). Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News that night that an unnamed tech-industry source believed AI could be behind the outages (Fortune; Cybernews).
- Tue 17 Nov, Apple: AppleCare on Device was unavailable for all users from 11:15 a.m. ET (16:15 UK) and was resolved at 3:39 p.m. ET (20:39 UK); iCloud sign-in problems began around 11:45 a.m. ET (16:45 UK) (AppleInsider; CBS). Apple said 'many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning' and that the outages were not a cyberattack (AppleInsider; MacRumors). At about 5:46 p.m. ET (22:46 UK) an Apple spokesperson told CBS services were 'green across the board' (CBS). Downdetector recorded around 2,300 Apple Pay and 1,800 iCloud user reports in the US at peak (Reuters via Dawn; iThome). iThome reports the disruption lasted more than six hours (translated from Chinese). Apple retail stores were also reported affected (MacRumors, citing Bloomberg).
- Tue 17 Nov, also: NSA's internal classified network (NSANet) was reported down by CNN, citing six people. The NSA said it 'experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance' and that mission-critical capabilities remained operational (CNN; Newsweek; Euronews). Marriott users reported technology issues (AP via PBS). Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business the outages were not a cyberattack; CNN and CBS report that Clayton linked the NSA outage to applying a software patch for PHP vulnerabilities, and CBS reports sources linking the outage to urgent PHP patching.
- Wed 18 Nov: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Manila, said there was 'zero evidence' that the incidents were related or caused by 'nefarious actors' (Euronews). At a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Clayton, Mullin and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia said there was no indication of a linked or malicious cyber activity (CBS; The Record). Vice President JD Vance cancelled a DealBook Summit appearance to attend meetings on the outages (CNBC). A senior administration official on a background call said officials have 'a great deal of confidence' the incidents stem from upgrades, patching and hardware changes (CNBC).
sections.technical:
No CVEs, ATT&CK techniques, malware or IOCs were identified in any of the published statements read for these incidents.

**Apple:** cause given only as an 'internal update'; Apple has not published a root cause. AppleInsider, citing an anonymous source in a Bloomberg report, said internal employee systems (AppleWeb, AppleConnect and remote-worker VPN access) also failed; Apple has not confirmed this.

**Other stated causes:** Microsoft - a latent defect from a July gateway-server update, with a surge in load and reduced capacity (preliminary report, per The Next Web and Cybernews). FAA - a router replacement by L3Harris; Cybernews cites a probe detail that a misconfigured broadcast feature generated about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, and CBS reports officials saying the replaced router flooded other routers (the specific 1,000 figure appears only in Cybernews). JPMorgan - a software bug in on-premises hardware systems (AP). NSA - 'scheduled routine maintenance' (NSA statement); Clayton's PHP-patching account is described above.

**Context:** Reuters cites Marsh data that clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October against 48 in the last two weeks of May.
sections.guidance:
Only what has been published by the organisations concerned:

- Apple (to media): systems restored; the outages were not a cyberattack.
- NSA (statement): mission-critical capabilities remain operational and infrastructure has multiple layers of redundancy (CNN; Emol, quoting its statement to EFE).
- DHS Secretary Mullin (House hearing, per The Record): DHS will hold a call with private-sector representatives about informing customers in advance when upgrades are coming; he said the government is not pressuring industry.
- Officials encouraged companies to communicate better with the public when carrying out large-scale software updates (SC World, summarising Nextgov).
sections.differing:
**Linked / cyber?** Rubio ('zero evidence'), Clayton ('These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack'), Raia ('no indication whatsoever' of malicious cyber activity; FBI cyber teams involved 'from day one') and Mullin ('98 percent confident' the incidents are not adversary activity) say no. Apple, Microsoft, United, JPMorgan and Marriott have said their outages were not cyber-related (AP, PBS). Sen. Josh Hawley (R) said 'If this is all a coincidence, it's like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world' (Reuters). House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said it was 'too premature' to conclude malicious activity but called for a congressional briefing (CNBC). Rep. Dan Goldman pressed Clayton on whether the NSA disruption was internal or external and said Clayton was 'clearly not answering my direct questions' (CBS).

**AI?** Mullin said on Fox News that an unnamed tech-industry source believed AI could be responsible; Fortune and Cybernews note the single unnamed source. At the hearing Mullin said he was '98 percent confident' the outages were not adversary activity. A senior administration official told CNBC it was 'challenging' to say how far AI was involved across the incidents. Microsoft attributed its outage to a software defect, extra load and reduced gateway capacity, not AI (Cybernews). Cybernews quotes UST's Adnan Masood saying the evidence does not point to rogue AI causing the disruptions. TJ Marlin of Guardrail Technologies says rogue AI agents did not cause the Microsoft outage, but automated health checks failed (Cybernews). Exabeam's Steve Povolny said the incidents were most likely coincidental (Computer Weekly). Sen. Mark Warner said 'the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity' (Computer Weekly; Digital Journal). Gary Marcus, an AI critic, told Fortune: 'I doubt we are getting full candor for these incidents' (opinion). Roman Yampolskiy wrote on X about an 'increasingly unsettling possibility' of AI playing a major role (Cybernews; social post).

**Duration:** iThome reports more than six hours of disruption; the AppleCare and iCloud times above are from AppleInsider and CBS.
sections.unknown:
Apple's root cause and the nature of the 'internal update'; whether any automation or AI tooling was involved; whether Apple will publish a post-incident report; the final FAA root cause; the NSA cause beyond its 'scheduled routine maintenance' statement (Clayton's PHP-patching account is not confirmed by the NSA); whether any shared dependency links the incidents; what the planned DHS call with industry produces. Apple's status page is script-rendered and its event-level times were not readable, so Apple timings above come from AppleInsider and CBS. Bloomberg, Sky News and AFP original texts were not read.

**Label basis:** Outages are confirmed by the affected organisations (Apple statement and status data as reported by AppleInsider and CBS; NSA statement) and by multiple outlets. 'No cyberattack / not linked' is the stated position of Apple, other companies, DNI, DHS and FBI on the record and is not independently verified; the AI/patching causal link is an UNCONFIRMED CLAIM.

items.headline: Microsoft attributes its 12–13 Nov Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online outage to a latent July gateway-server defect; outage-themed phishing followed
items.summary: Microsoft's preliminary report attributes the 12–13 Nov Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online outage to a latent defect in a July fix for M365 networking gateway servers, combined with a Teams failover and about 14% reduced gateway capacity; more than 80% of gateway servers became unresponsive. Microsoft says it was not a cyberattack; Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported an outage-themed phishing campaign observed on 13 Nov.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.firstReported: 12 Nov 16:20 UK (Microsoft-stated start 11.20 EST, per Infosecurity Magazine)

sections.happened:
All times UK (GMT) unless stated.

**12 Nov (Thu):** Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online disruption begins; the Microsoft-stated start is 11.20 EST, i.e. 16:20 UK (Infosecurity Magazine). Per Microsoft's preliminary report as relayed by iTnews, Teams failed over to the primary network gateway, which also serves Exchange Online, about 15 hours before the outage.

**13 Nov (Fri):** Microsoft says it was "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents" that was "introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change" (statement quoted by TNW). The Register reports a mitigation, an update reverting the defective change, applied from 07:20 UTC, and Microsoft confirmed healthy service at 16:10 UTC. Infosecurity Magazine gives 'over 22 hours' with service fully restored at 23:15 EST.

**14 Nov:** Microsoft issues its final customer update at 04:15 (The Register; time zone not stated).

**15 Nov:** Microsoft publishes a preliminary post-incident report (The Register).

**16 Nov (Mon):** Charles Lamanna, Executive Vice President of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posts an abridged version of the report on X (ABC News).

**18 Nov (Wed):** In an interview on CNBC's Mad Money, Satya Nadella says: "It was one of those crazy perfect storms where there was a latent bug that got sort of found only during a particular traffic pattern... Of course, we should have done the testing before" (CNBC). CNBC reports Microsoft shares had pulled back nearly 9% over the two weeks since their all-time closing high on 4 Nov.
sections.technical:
No CVE, CVSS or exploitation is associated with the outage. Root cause as stated in Microsoft's preliminary report and relayed by The Register, iTnews, The Stack and TNW:

1. **Latent defect:** lock contention inside an internal process on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers, which made servers unresponsive under certain load conditions. The defect came from a fix prepared for M365 gateway servers, deployed from July, and sat undetected for more than three months (iTnews; The Register). Load testing focused on weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores; the contention was worse on newer machines with more cores (iTnews; The Stack).
2. **Load increase:** about 15 hours before the outage, Teams failed over to the primary gateway that also serves Exchange Online (iTnews).
3. **Reduced capacity:** nearly 14% of gateway server capacity was out of service because of an unrelated issue the previous day; Microsoft said this reduction "had no impact on its own" (ABC News).

**Cascade:** the defect was encountered across the fleet in less than two hours; at its lowest more than 80% of servers were unresponsive (The Stack, quoting Lamanna). Normal bulkheads did not contain the cascade because of a "separate issue" that Microsoft has not described (The Stack).

**Recovery:** restored servers were immediately swamped by waiting traffic, and Microsoft's automated recovery was not designed for such a broad failure (TNW; iTnews). Normal rollback, flighting and feature flags could not quickly revert the change because of the latent bug; engineers applied an update returning the code path to a known good state to large blocks of servers, in some cases more than half a region (iTnews).

**Phishing campaign:** Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a "coordinated, high volume" phishing campaign on 13 Nov using lures themed on the outage (Infosecurity Magazine, citing Microsoft's blog dated 16 Nov). Infosecurity Magazine reports Microsoft's assessment that the aim was likely credential phishing; it reports 'no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity' and no named threat actor or malware family.
sections.guidance: Microsoft said a final post-incident review would provide more detail 'later this week' (Lamanna, per iTnews). The Register and TNW report that Microsoft plans to publish its final post-incident report on 20 November.
sections.differing:
**Cause:** Microsoft says the incident was 'not related to cyber or AI / agents' (13 Nov statement, per TNW). Its 13 Nov statement attributed the incident to 'an earlier network capacity upgrade' following a recent network change; its preliminary report (15 Nov) attributes it to a July fix for M365 gateway servers combined with a Teams failover and reduced capacity. The sources read do not reconcile these two descriptions (TNW; The Register).

**Duration:** Infosecurity Magazine gives 'over 22 hours' with restoration at 23:15 EST on 13 Nov; The Register's timeline gives a mitigation at 07:20 UTC and healthy confirmation at 16:10 UTC on 13 Nov.

**October updates:** The Stack reports that Microsoft did not tie the incident to October 2026 Windows Server updates, which The Stack says caused similar downstream problems for customers.
sections.unknown:
Content of the final post-incident report (due 20 Nov). The 'separate issue' that stopped bulkheads from containing the cascade. Why about 14% of gateway capacity was out of service the previous day. How the 13 Nov 'network capacity upgrade' wording relates to the July-defect account. Whether any phishing recipients entered credentials (Microsoft has not confirmed credential capture). Congressional interest: House Homeland Security Committee chair Andrew Garbarino told Politico he was seeking information from Microsoft and CISA (per TNW). Any financial or contractual remedies.

Label basis: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED. Microsoft acknowledged the outage and published the preliminary root cause (relayed by The Register, iTnews, The Stack, TNW and ABC News); the root cause rests on Microsoft's own account with no independent technical verification. The phishing campaign is described by Infosecurity Magazine from Microsoft's blog.

items.headline: FAA pauses Juniper router rollout after nationwide ground stop; root cause still undetermined
items.summary: The FAA says data flooding its FTI network from two sites (about 1,000 connection attempts every 4–5 seconds) caused the 13 Nov nationwide ground stop; it disabled a function on more than 60 Juniper routers and paused installs. HPE says its equipment worked as configured, and the root cause is still undetermined.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.firstReported: 13 Nov (ground stop); Juniper pause reported 17 Nov

sections.happened:
**Fri 13 Nov, ~20:30 UK (about 3:30pm ET):** the FAA says its legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network at about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Instability hit 17 of 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and spread into several TRACONs. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop "out of an abundance of caution". It says about 3,500 aircraft were airborne and all landed safely.

**Sat 14 Nov, ~01:15 UK (8:15pm ET on Fri 13 Nov):** the FAA says the system was stable and air traffic resumed. At a press conference that day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford briefed reporters (ABC News photo caption). Duffy said L3Harris, the FAA's network service provider, was doing a routine switch from copper to fibre at a remote site when a router began flooding the network (CNN, Reuters). CNN reports investigators were determining whether the fault was defective equipment or an installation or configuration error.

**Sun 15 Nov:** the FAA published a Q&A. It names a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas as the two potential sources. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including deploying a new router. L3Harris blocked both locations and the network stabilised. The broadcasting function was disabled on all new routers. The FAA says it disabled "the same functionality" on more than 60 other Juniper routers "and we have paused installing them". The Q&A says the event was "due to the legacy TDM system causing instabilities" and not the modernisation work. It reports approximately 12,462 cancellations on 13 Nov, 9,082 of them by major airlines, and says not all were directly caused by the ground stop.

**Mon 16 Nov:** Duffy gave a CNBC interview (per Network World). He said "those routers in my system didn't go down" and that "2001 Cisco servers" which "went out of commission in 2006" were flooded.

**Tue 17 Nov:** Duffy and Bedford briefed senators. Duffy said it was the 69th installation of that router, and the previous 68 had gone well. Reuters reports he said investigators had recreated the El Dorado behaviour at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida with the FAA, Cisco and the FBI on site, and that "we don't have clarity yet" on the root cause. The FAA confirmed the installation pause to CNN and Network World; CNN attributes the first report of the pause to The Wall Street Journal. The FAA did not say how long the pause will last. The same day, all 13 Democratic members of the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, sent a letter (ABC News reports it was sent on Tuesday). It asks for an immediate pause on further Juniper deployment until the FAA shows improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover and rollback procedures, and asks for a joint technical briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper and written information by 23 Nov.

**Scale:** the letter, citing L3Harris, says 3,648 routers are to be converted to Juniper devices, with 400 installed and 69 operational. Reported cancellation totals differ: the FAA's 12,462 (13 Nov only), "more than 18,000" (Reuters) and "more than 17,000" (DCD).
sections.technical:
**Mechanism as stated by the FAA:** data flooding from two sites, the El Dorado radio communications site and the Amarillo radar site, overloaded the FTI network at about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds. The FAA says the broadcasting function was disabled on the originating Juniper routers and on more than 60 other Juniper routers. Duffy said the El Dorado router, once it began broadcasting into the network, overloaded it (Reuters). No CVE, vulnerability, threat actor or malware has been identified. The FAA says that "based on all available evidence, we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor."

**Unverified source detail:** Network World quotes an anonymous "source close to the investigation" who says the Juniper device is a circuit-to-packet device translating between analogue copper and IP, that its multicast feature is sold turned off and must be configured, and that it is "premature" to say the Juniper device flooded the network because receiving devices' behaviour also matters. DCD, citing an unnamed source, says the broadcast feature should have been off because the device was communicating with a network of 20-year-old Cisco 600 Series routers. Neither account is confirmed by the FAA or the vendors.

**Legacy gear:** Reuters reports the FAA said the Cisco routers being replaced were produced in 2001 and were due for replacement in 2006.

**Testing:** Duffy said the FAA spent a year testing Juniper routers at its technical centre (Reuters). The senators' letter says a sample passed pre-deployment testing and questions whether that testing reflected operating conditions.

**Outside views:** Network World quotes Stairwell CTO Mike Wiacek, who says he cannot say for certain whether it was a cyber attack and that four major outages in under a week look suspicious. NetBox Labs CEO Kris Beevers says there is no indication that anything malicious happened and that network configuration changes often look like an internal denial-of-service. Both are opinions.
sections.guidance:
**FAA (Q&A, 15 Nov):** it disabled the broadcasting functionality on the originating Juniper routers and on more than 60 other Juniper routers, and paused installing them. It said it will "reevaluate when we do replacement/maintenance work" because the work was done mid-day. It told Network World on 17 Nov that it has paused installation of the Juniper router and did not say how long the pause will last.

**Senate Commerce Committee Democrats (letter, sent 17 Nov per ABC News):** request an immediate pause on further Juniper deployment, with resumption conditional on improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover and rollback procedures, and a briefing to Congress before resumption. They ask for an initial safety assessment of operational Juniper devices by 23 Nov.

**HPE:** no advisory, bulletin or fix has been published. Its statements are set out under differing accounts.
sections.differing:
**FAA/DOT vs Juniper-first framing:** the FAA Q&A attributes the event to "the legacy TDM system causing instabilities" and says the modernisation work did not cause it. The same document says the flooding was traced to a new Juniper router at El Dorado and that the broadcasting function was disabled on all new routers. The senators' letter says the DOT attributed the disruption to "old switches [and] old routers," "when in fact the deployment of the new Juniper routers seem to be the problem," and describes this as a discrepancy with the FAA's contractor. At the Senate on 17 Nov, Duffy said of the 69th router: "This was the one that started to behave this way" (per DCD).

**HPE:** says "Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured," and that "the FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause" (CNN, Reuters). DCD reports HPE told it the device functioned as configured by the installer and did not fail or act improperly.

**Cause of fault:** Duffy said on 14 Nov that it was not determined whether this was contractor installation error or faulty equipment (CNN, Reuters). CNN reports the FAA monitored the L3Harris engineer during the installation, per FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.

**L3Harris:** says it has completed more than 70% of the planned copper-to-fibre conversion with its telco partners and the FAA (Network World). The FAA Q&A calls L3Harris the FAA's current network service provider.

**Funding context:** ABC News reports the Department of Transportation submitted a $50.1 billion budget request for air traffic control on 17 Nov, up from $30 billion; the senators' letter criticises that increase.

**Consistent across sources read:** the flooding at two sites, the 17 of 22 centres affected, the ground stop and the installation pause. The cause is not established.
sections.unknown:
- Root cause: officials recreated the El Dorado behaviour but had not established the root cause as of 17 Nov (Reuters, CNN). It is not known whether the cause is hardware, firmware, software behaviour, configuration, installation, or interaction with the legacy network.
- Who or what enabled the broadcast/multicast function on the device, and why its effect reached 17 of 22 centres.
- Whether other Juniper routers carry the same risk beyond the disabled function. The FAA has not said when installation resumes or how long the pause will last.
- The device type: sources differ (router, circuit-to-packet device, copper-to-fibre media converter), and the FAA has not confirmed any of these.
- Final cancellation count: the FAA's 12,462 covers 13 Nov only; Reuters and DCD report higher totals.
- Whether L3Harris, HPE or Cisco will publish findings, and whether the FAA will meet the senators' 23 Nov deadline.
- Not read for this brief: the DOT's own briefing pages (returned access denied).

**Label basis:** FAA primary Q&A and statements, the Senate letter, and reports by Reuters, CNN, ABC News, Network World, DCD, The Stack and iTWire confirm the ground stop, the FAA's preliminary flooding account and the installation pause. The root cause is not established and is not part of the label.

items.headline: NSA classified internal network (NSANet) disrupted for a second day; DNI links it to PHP patching; officials see no sign of a cyberattack
items.summary: NSANet went down on 17 Nov; NSA cites "scheduled routine maintenance", the DNI links it on the record to PHP patching that left systems not restarting, and officials say there is no sign of a cyberattack; restoration was still under way on 18 Nov, when CBS reported NSANet back up with staggered arrivals continuing.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
**Tue 17 Nov.** Morning: an NSA employee voicemail inbox described a "code yellow" (second-highest of three levels) with staggered arrivals at Fort Meade, Maryland, per CNN, which credits the New York Times with first reporting that detail (NYT not read). CNN published at 15:31 UK, reporting NSANet down per six people familiar. CBS News separately reported the network offline per multiple U.S. officials.

Tuesday afternoon: NSA statement (quoted by CNN and CBS; the nsa.gov page could not be read): "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance", some internal systems affected, mission-critical capabilities "fully operational", infrastructure has "multiple layers of redundancy". Also Tuesday afternoon, DNI Jay Clayton told Fox Business that patching following PHP vulnerabilities "has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today" (quote as carried by CBS and CNN). Clayton and senior administration officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack.

Tuesday evening (CNN, citing the voicemail inbox and a source): the inbox reverted to "code green" (report as scheduled), then later moved to "code orange", closing the campus to most employees until further notice. The Record's source says non-essential staff received a "Code Gray" notice late Tuesday to arrive at 10:00 Wednesday. CBS sources said some activities were redirected to other NSA facilities.

**Wed 18 Nov.** The Record: arrival time slipped to the afternoon; the network was working but staff arrivals stayed staggered because login is the most taxing process; one source speculated full restoration might take "another day or two"; campus cafeteria closed. CNN saw an operational update telling Maryland non-essential day-shift staff not to report unless directed, and a senior administration official said restoration patching was going "slower than expected". CNN (four sources) reported the disruption also affected NSA Georgia (Fort Gordon, Augusta), which supports Middle East signals-intelligence and cyber operations; staff there could not use NSANet to reach colleagues deployed in the region and used workarounds and backup systems. Nextgov: the network was still facing issues Wednesday, staff received rolling guidance on when to report. Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee he has a "very high level of confidence" that none of the recent outages (NSA, FAA, Microsoft and others) was a cyberattack, calling them separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a red team and a report to Congress by 1 Dec (The Record).

**Late 18 Nov.** CBS (published 18 Nov, 5:28 PM EST): two sources say NSANet is back up and running, but "Code Gray" staggered arrivals continue over fears the system cannot handle everyone logging in at once, and personnel are asked to delay non-essential tasks. iThome (translated from Traditional Chinese) and DigitalToday repeat the CBS account. No NSA statement later than 17 Nov appears in the reporting cited.

Scale: Fort Meade has more than 20,000 employees (CNN). CNN also reported that a Five Eyes partner source and a former US intelligence official said intelligence sharing with allies was not affected, and that a current and a former US official said communication of urgent intelligence to the President (travelling in Asia) was not affected.
sections.technical:
**Root cause as stated.** Clayton (on the record, Fox Business): patching after a PHP vulnerability left some systems not coming back up after patching. NSA's own wording is only "scheduled routine maintenance"; neither NSA nor Clayton named a CVE in the quotes read. CBS identifies the PHP vulnerabilities as the PHP2Shell pair, disclosed last month (CNN refers to PHP vulnerabilities without naming them); The Record's source and two people cited by Nextgov said Clayton's remarks were accurate. The specific NSANet systems, versions, and failure mechanism are not public.

**PHP2Shell background (published by others).** CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), described by CISA as allowing unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP. Fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (released 21 Oct 2026); minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 (Help Net Security). Reported exploitation: Amazon recorded an attempt on 17 Oct, before disclosure; The Hacker News reports that Cloudflare saw attempts rise sharply and that Sophos and Arctic Wolf reported attempts to install a Mirai variant, which had so far failed. A separate issue, CVE-2026-115560, concerns session upload progress with an uncommon configuration (The Hacker News, 23 Oct).

No ATT&CK techniques, threat actor, malware or IOCs are attributed to the NSA outage, since officials describe it as a self-inflicted maintenance failure. The Georgia-hub impact and "code" alert levels come from anonymous sources and a voicemail recording seen by CNN.
sections.guidance:
**FBI, NSA and CISA** issued urgent warnings on 21 Oct 2026 directing organisations to patch PHP2Shell immediately (CBS News). **CISA** (alert, 21 Oct) said organisations that cannot update immediately, or that use PHP 8.1 or earlier, should take PHP-based systems offline until patched or updated. The NSA advisory page could not be read.

**NSA on the outage:** only the 17 Nov statement quoted above. **Clayton:** attributes it to maintenance/patching; says no TTPs of an attack were observed. **DHS Secretary Mullin** (Nextgov): DHS is convening a call with industry.
sections.differing:
**Cause.** NSA says "scheduled routine maintenance"; Clayton ties it to PHP patching; CBS sources said routine system patching; The Record and Nextgov sources call Clayton's account accurate. CNN's officials said it was not a cyberattack but connected to PHP update handling. No on-record contradiction was found. Schumer said it is "too coincidental" and asked for a red team to challenge the assumption (The Record). Clayton said he has a "very high level of confidence" that the recent outages were not cyberattacks, because they had different causes and showed none of the attack techniques he cited (CNN; The Record). The evidence he cites is not public.

**Severity and duration.** NSA's statement describes "temporary degradation" with mission-critical capabilities operational. Anonymous sources told CNN the agency closed its campus to most staff for at least two days, the Georgia hub lost NSANet, and a senior official said restoration was slower than expected; a former senior NSA official described it as "alarming, but likely not crippling". The two accounts are not strictly incompatible; NSA has not addressed the closure or Georgia reporting publicly.

**Status.** CBS sources: back up and running (CBS, 18 Nov). Nextgov: still facing issues Wednesday. The Record: working but throttled by login load. The New York Times, per UPI, cited a source saying NSANet had been unstable for weeks (NYT and UPI-relayed; not independently verified, and not in NSA's account).

**Timing of patching.** Clayton said the PHP update was about 10 days earlier (CBS quote); the PHP fixes were released 21 Oct, about four weeks earlier. Which patches NSA was applying on 17 Nov has not been stated.
sections.unknown:
Exact systems and failure mechanism; whether the specific patches were PHP2Shell fixes (named by CNN/CBS, not by NSA); how many staff and facilities remain affected and when normal operations resume; why the 'code' level was relaxed then tightened on Tuesday; whether any data or classified work was lost or delayed; whether NSA will issue a further statement; whether Congress or inspectors general will review. The stated no-cyberattack position rests on official assurances and anonymous sources, with no published forensic evidence. One derivative report could not be read, so any attribution taken from it is unverified.

**Label basis:** NSA's own statement (17 Nov, quoted by CNN, CBS and UPI) acknowledges 'temporary degradation' of internal systems; the DNI's PHP-patching explanation is on the record; CNN, CBS News, The Record, Nextgov and UPI report the disruption. Scope, duration and status rest on anonymous sources.

items.headline: Pakistan internet slowdown linked to SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) submarine cable fault, PTA says
items.summary: Pakistan's regulator PTA said on 18 Nov that SMW5 has a fault about 11 km off Pakistan's shore causing intermittent connectivity and slower service; traffic is being rerouted and no restoration time has been given.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened:
18 Nov 2026 (Wed): PTA said in a statement, posted on X and reproduced by outlets, that the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) cable system had reported a fault about 11 km from Pakistan's shore, which may cause some internet users to experience intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality. Transworld Associates (TWA) is coordinating with the SMW5 Consortium on the root cause and an estimated time for restoration; traffic is being rerouted via alternative international links (Dawn, 21:13 PKT = 16:13 UK; Dialogue Pakistan, 21:39 PKT).

Same day, NetBlocks said the incident was consistent with a fault on the SMW5 system, with operators attempting to establish alternative routes (Dawn). The National and Arab Times attribute to Cloudflare Radar a drop in HTTP traffic of as much as 36%; NextUp News attributes the same 36% figure to NetBlocks.

Arab Times (19 Nov, 10:42 +03:00) reports that a High Commission notice announced the temporary suspension of NADRA, passport and visa services in London because of internet disruption that it attributes to the SMW5 fault. No other source read confirms this.

Dawn reports a previous SMW5 fault on 1 July 2026 that caused widespread connectivity problems, resolved on 3 July.
sections.technical: SMW5 (SEA-ME-WE 5) international submarine cable system; fault approx. 11 km from Pakistan shore (PTA). Root cause not identified as of the latest reports read. No CVE, vendor advisory or IOCs apply; no attack is attributed by any source read.
sections.guidance: PTA (as quoted): will continue to monitor and facilitate the earliest possible restoration of normal internet services. No user-facing instructions were published in the statements read.
sections.differing:
PTA: 'may cause some internet users to experience intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality'.

NetBlocks (quoted in Dawn): 'consistent with a fault on the SMW5 international subsea cable system with operators now attempting to establish alternative routes'. Dawn also reports NetBlocks confirming a decline in connectivity that caused slow service.

Cloudflare Radar (as reported by The National and Arab Times): HTTP data dropped by as much as 36%. NextUp News attributes the same figure to NetBlocks.

Headlines vary: The News ('Submarine cable fault disrupts internet across country: PTA') and Dialogue Pakistan ('PTA says fault in submarine cable may slow internet in Pakistan').
sections.unknown:
Root cause of the fault; estimated time for restoration (not announced in any statement read); how many users are affected (PTA did not specify); whether the London NADRA and visa suspension is confirmed by the High Commission or any other source (Arab Times is the only source read for the link). The 1 July restoration notice was not read.

**Label basis:** PTA statement as reproduced by Dawn, Dialogue Pakistan, APP, The News and others (PTA's website not read); NetBlocks observation as quoted in Dawn; the cable fault cause is not stated.

items.headline: European Commission hit by cyberattack on internal HR and staff systems
items.summary: Politico reported on 19 Nov that the European Commission is responding to a cyberattack on individual internal systems, including the Sysper HR platform, that may have exposed staff personal data; exposure is not confirmed.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.firstReported: 19 Nov 07:16 UK time (Echo FM, timed 10:16 Moscow time; earliest outlet read)

sections.happened:
Politico reported the attack on Thursday 19 Nov 2026 (Politico itself not read; relayed by Euronews, Yle, The Next Web, Novaya Gazeta Europe and Echo FM). Per the relayed reports, the attack has run for about ten days and the Commission took several systems offline as a precaution, including Sysper (payslips, leave, timesheets), the MyPMO medical-reimbursement service and translation services. Sysper and MyPMO returned early in the week, but Sysper failed again on Wednesday 18 Nov (Novaya Gazeta Europe). Euronews, citing an anonymous official on Thursday, says Sysper was working again while the health-insurance scheme JSIS remained unavailable. Technology chief Henna Virkkunen briefed commissioners on Wednesday 18 Nov. Euronews reports that CERT-EU is assessing the damage and officials had not yet received official internal communications.

As background, the Commission had two earlier 2026 incidents: a March compromise of the AWS account supporting the europa.eu hosting, in which CERT-EU said about 92GB of compressed data was taken (The Record, 3 Apr 2026), and a January attack on the central mobile-device management infrastructure (Euronews, TNW).
sections.technical: No technical details for the November incident were published by CERT-EU or the Commission in the sources read. Politico, relayed by Novaya Gazeta Europe and The Next Web, reports that CERT-EU detected in early November that hackers used ARTEX, a publicly available AI-driven penetration-testing framework. CERT-EU's own blog of 5 Nov 2026 ('From Penetration Testing to Cyber Threat: Beware of ARTEX') says several threat actors worldwide have used ARTEX to automate campaigns and that it has observed similar AI-driven activity against its constituency, 'highly likely' involving ARTEX. That advisory does not name the Commission incident.
sections.differing: Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier (via Politico): individual systems were targeted; necessary steps taken; affected people informed (relayed by Yle, TNW, Novaya). An anonymous EU official (via Politico): the Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, but the scale of damage is unclear (relayed by TNW, Novaya, Yle). Yle, citing Reuters: the Commission did not respond to a Reuters request for comment early on Thursday. Euronews describes a 'major cyberattack'. Euronews describes the disruption as 'relatively minor'. Staff Politico spoke to, as relayed by Novaya Gazeta Europe, mostly received salaries on time, but some could not submit timesheets or leave requests.
sections.unknown:
Whether attackers accessed or exfiltrated staff personal data from Sysper, JSIS or other HR systems. Who is behind the attack (no attribution by the Commission or CERT-EU was found; the ARTEX link is a Politico-sourced claim). The full scope of affected systems. Whether the Commission's internal documents were touched (Euronews notes they are hosted separately).

**Label basis:** Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier's on-record confirmation that 'individual systems were targeted' and that the Commission took steps (as reported by Politico and relayed by TNW and Yle); data exposure and attribution remain unconfirmed.

items.headline: Equinor confirms ongoing cyberattack on some IT systems; says production unaffected and no data theft indicated
items.summary: Norway's state-owned Equinor says an ongoing cyberattack hit certain IT systems, that it is not a virus attack, that production is unaffected and that no data theft is indicated; the attacker is unidentified.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
17 Nov 2026, 17:55 UK (18:55 CET): Equinor posts a statement that it has detected an ongoing cyberattack against certain IT systems, that relevant resources are mobilised, and that there are no indications data was stolen and production is unaffected. NRK carries it the same evening. NRK reports the first version of the release said employees might see disruption to some services; those sentences were later removed.

18 Nov (UK morning; the time is not shown on Equinor's page, and Riviera puts it just over 12 hours after the first statement): Equinor update says it has a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems are affected; not a virus attack, so no risk of spreading; no indication of consequences for employees, partners or suppliers; production remains unaffected. The Record reports it as a Wednesday update.

19 Nov, 10:40 UK (11:40 CET): Equinor update says the attack is still ongoing, restoration time is unknown, production runs as normal, there are no indications data was stolen or altered, and the attack 'does not appear to be specifically targeting Equinor'. The company says it is in continuous contact with national security authorities and has reported the matter to the police.

Other parties (as reported): Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) says it is aware and ready to help; NSM raised Norway's cyber threat level to the second-highest of five levels on 27 Oct (Riviera, Security Affairs). EnergyWatch reports, in a headline only, that Aker BP is stepping up preparedness after the attack; the article text was not read.
sections.technical: Equinor has not published an attack vector, ATT&CK mapping, CVEs, indicators of compromise or the start date. Its statement says the attack is 'not a virus attack' and so there is no risk of it spreading (Equinor, 18 Nov). Riviera notes this suggests self-propagating malware is unlikely; that is Riviera's inference, not Equinor's words.
sections.guidance: Equinor (company statement, 17 Nov and 19 Nov): 'Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity'; it reports the matter to the police and to national security authorities. NSM (per Security Affairs and Riviera): it is aware of the attack and ready to support. No further statement from authorities appears in the sources reviewed.
sections.differing: Equinor: no indication data was stolen; production unaffected (Equinor statement, 17-19 Nov). Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk to EnergyWatch: the no-data statement covers all types of data, including GDPR data (EnergyWatch teaser). Reuters, citing an unnamed source at Equinor: the internal email system was down (reported by The Record and Riviera; not confirmed by Equinor in its statement). Skjelsbæk to NTB (per NRK and The Record): employees may have problems with some corporate applications and IT services, but the company still has access to its systems. An EnergyWatch cyber-security adviser (name not given in the teaser) said the attackers are 'partially in control' and that the integrity of several IT systems has been breached; this is one outside expert's assessment, not a finding.
sections.unknown:
Who carried out the attack and why: no group named by Equinor, NSM or police; Security Affairs says separate claims from August (a pro-Russian group that claimed an August attack on Norwegian government digital services) do not establish who is behind this attack. How access was gained, when it began, which systems and how many are affected, how long restoration will take, and whether the attack is linked to the Aker BP preparedness report (no link stated by any party reviewed). Whether the reported email outage is accurate; Equinor has not confirmed it.

**Label basis:** Equinor's own website statement (17 Nov, with updates on 18 and 19 Nov) confirms the attack; its claims on production and data are company statements, not independently verified.

items.headline: Russian espionage group Cold Relic (Star Blizzard) uses cloud data from one US breach to compromise a second US organisation
items.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant report that Russia-nexus group COLD RELIC, also tracked as Star Blizzard, used data and identities taken from a late-2025 breach of one US organisation to impersonate an employee and compromise a second US organisation's Entra ID-federated Google Workspace account in 2026.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
17 Nov 2026: Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant publish 'COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise' (Google Cloud blog, dated 17 Nov per Infosecurity Magazine; The Record says published Wednesday).

Late 2025: COLD RELIC uses a US residential proxy near the victim, stolen Super Admin credentials and an MFA push-fatigue attack against a US organisation's Google Workspace tenant. It then downloads the drive contents, exports employee lists and runs a domain-wide Google Workspace Customer Takeout, and remains in the tenant for several months (Google).

2026: after the group was removed, it sends emails impersonating employees of the first organisation. Separately, in a second US organisation's intrusion, it contacts a target via an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee of the first organisation, then sends phishing links for Entra ID credentials and tokens. It registers a new MFA device in the SSO layer and bulk-downloads files from the user's cloud drive (Google; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News).

Google says it has seen new COLD RELIC phishing operations as recently as November 2026 (Google, via Infosecurity).
sections.technical:
Tactics as described by GTIG/Mandiant (no CVEs cited):
- Initial access: residential proxy network geolocated near the victim; stolen Super Admin credentials; MFA push-notification fatigue (Google).
- Persistence: rogue MFA devices, passkeys and MFA backup codes; passkeys persisted across password and session resets (Google).
- Defence impairment: queried admin security investigation and email audit logs, viewed/modified/deleted Alert Center notifications; Google's report lists MITRE ATT&CK T1562.008 (Impair Defenses) and T1082 (System Information Discovery) for these behaviours.
- Collection: mass sharing to an attacker-controlled email account, direct downloads, Customer Takeout, OAuth-based email sync (Google).
- Lures: compromised websites as redirectors with a parameter referencing the prior victim; VirusTotal submission of a redirector in June 2026 (Google).
Google says the group selects proxies geolocated to the victim's approximate location to avoid impossible-travel alerts.
sections.guidance: Google/Mandiant's case study includes detection and hardening recommendations for defenders; they are not reproduced here.
sections.differing: Google describes the group as a Russian state-sponsored threat group and says the US Department of Justice has assessed it operates within Russia's FSB (Google's citation of the DOJ assessment). The Record: 'U.S. authorities have linked the group to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).' SecurityWeek: 'formally associated by the US with Russia's intelligence service FSB'. Naming: Google uses COLD RELIC (formerly COLDRIVER, UNC4057; also Star Blizzard, Callisto, Gossamer Bear); Infosecurity and The Hacker News treat Star Blizzard and Cold Relic as one cluster per Google. The Record calls the group 'state-backed' per Google's research. No party disputed the findings in sources read.
sections.unknown:
Identities of the two US victim organisations (not disclosed). What data was taken from the second organisation and how much (not disclosed). Whether the late-2025 data was sold or used beyond these two intrusions. Whether the 2026 activity is linked to any other reported Star Blizzard operations. Exact dates of the 2026 intrusion beyond 'a 2026 compromise'. Independent confirmation of the FSB link beyond the US assessment as cited by Google.

**Label basis:** Google/Mandiant incident-response case study (blog dated 17 Nov 2026) is the primary source; both victim organisations are unnamed and no victim or government statement was found; the state link is Google's assessment citing a US DOJ view.

items.headline: Agentic AI pentest framework ARTEX used in attacks: Google GTIG and an FBI flash advisory report it; Barracuda's post-mortem reports a cloud intrusion using ARTEX
items.summary: Google GTIG (16 Nov) reports multi-agent offensive frameworks including ARTEX in use and says it suspects operations are approaching fully agentic intrusions; an FBI flash advisory cites ARTEX-linked campaigns since at least August 2026; Barracuda's post-mortem, as reported, attributes a roughly 44-hour cloud intrusion to ARTEX.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
October 2026: a third-party AI vendor's development environment was reportedly compromised; iThome says the attacker likely obtained a cloud access key there, which Barracuda had issued to that vendor and not revoked (iThome, citing Barracuda's disclosure).

1 Nov 2026, 04:33 UTC (same as UK time): attacker first used the key (iThome). Barracuda's post-mortem says the attacker reached about 10 cloud environments, including some supporting its XDR platform (Risky Business quoting Barracuda); iThome gives the window as 44 hours and Risky Business as 'almost two days'.

2 Nov 2026: attacker pushed short-lived branches to several code repositories to trigger build workflows and print build secrets to logs (iThome).

4 Nov 2026: Barracuda learned of the breach from the AI provider and after an engineer noticed unusual activity on their own account (Risky Business quoting Barracuda; iThome).

16 Nov 2026 (Monday): Google GTIG published its AI Threat Tracker, describing autonomous multi-agent frameworks including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI in use. TechCrunch (16 Nov, 17:36 UK time) reports the FBI flash advisory; Infosecurity Magazine (17 Nov) also reports it. ABC News (17 Nov) says the FBI alert was issued 'late last week'. KLTV (17 Nov, 18:50 UK time) reports the same advisory.
sections.technical:
The FBI advisory, as quoted by ABC News, says 'ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques'. KLTV reports that some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours (KLTV paraphrase; TechCrunch gives 'under three hours').

GTIG blog (16 Nov): these frameworks share capabilities including using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on demand and using real-time execution feedback to adjust tactics. GTIG also says threat actors may use LLMs to reverse-engineer patches (differential analysis) to weaponise n-day flaws. Separately, GTIG cites open-source research on PaperCut print-management servers exploited as zero-days in late August 2026, chained for unauthenticated remote code execution (CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078). GTIG says adversaries are 'trading stealth for velocity', leaving 'recognizable identifiers' and 'code-level traces'.

Infosecurity Magazine says frameworks like ARTEX manage sub-agents across kill-chain stages.

Barracuda (via Risky Business and iThome): attacker used an unrevoked cloud access key; accessed stored AWS access keys and an Azure service principal secret; reached Kubernetes clusters; attempted to create a new cloud admin identity (unsuccessful, per iThome); searched for crypto-wallet data. Barracuda reports finding no evidence that XDR customer integration credentials were accessed. Barracuda believes the intrusion was the work of a financially motivated group (Risky Business).

No CVE is attached to the ARTEX activity in the sources read. Barracuda patched a series of bugs around the same time that 'immediately entered active exploitation', but Barracuda says these do not appear to have been used in the intrusion (Risky Business).
sections.guidance:
FBI (as quoted by KLTV): recommends organisations review internet-facing systems, limit access to administrative tools, and monitor for unusual sign-ins and data transfers. The FBI says the original developer removed its public repository after public disclosure of malicious use in October, but copies and modified versions remain online.

Barracuda (as quoted by Risky Business): told some customers to reissue the same credentials out of precaution.
sections.differing:
Google GTIG (16 Nov blog) says it suspects these operations are approaching fully agentic intrusions and gives no timeframe. Infosecurity Magazine reports that Google expects such attacks 'in the next three to six months' (its headline says three months).

Barracuda describes the actor as financially motivated (Risky Business quoting Barracuda).

The FBI advisory, as quoted by KLTV, cites campaigns across sectors including financial services, government and telecommunications, and a South Korean financial institution with about 67,000 people's personal information exposed; TechCrunch reports at least 68,000 people for the South Korean financial-sector attacks.

TechCrunch reports the FBI confirmed Microsoft's findings that attackers used ARTEX against ConnectWise customers, with access to Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 customers; ConnectWise told TechCrunch it does not have the visibility to confirm the number of affected environments cited by the FBI. KLTV reports the advisory describes attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream environments and does not specify which were breached.
sections.unknown:
The FBI advisory's own text and reference number were not reviewed; coverage of it is via ABC News, KLTV and TechCrunch. The GTIG campaign list and IOCs beyond the blog summary were not reviewed in full. Barracuda's post-mortem was not reviewed directly; its account is taken from Risky Business and iThome. The third-party AI vendor is not named in the sources read.

**Label basis:** Barracuda's own post-mortem (as quoted in Risky Business and iThome) acknowledges the intrusion and ARTEX use; GTIG's assessment is taken from its published blog; the FBI advisory is taken from its quotation in ABC News, KLTV and TechCrunch (primary FBI document not reviewed).

items.headline: Coles Group investigating cyber security incident; no evidence of data compromise so far, operations unaffected
items.summary: Coles Group told the ASX on 16 November 2026 that it is investigating a cyber security incident, has found no evidence customer, team or supplier data was compromised or removed 'to date', and says stores and online trading are operating normally; a small number of customers report issues with Liquorland click-and-collect.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
16 Nov 2026 (AEDT), per the ASX release: Coles Group Limited (ASX:COL) announced "COLES INVESTIGATING CYBER SECURITY INCIDENT" to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The iTnews article is timestamped 9:11AM AEDT on 16 Nov 2026, which is 22:11 UK time on 15 Nov. ABC News published at 05:00 UTC (05:00 UK) on 16 Nov, saying the statement came Monday morning.

Coles' updates page (colesgroup.com.au/updates) reads "Current as at 16 November 2026, 8:30am" (Australian time, as shown).

Coles says it is working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and has engaged "global cyber security experts" to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment". ABC reports that a small number of customers are having issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which Coles is investigating. The Shout reports that Liquorland temporarily suspended click-and-collect and that its stores remain open with home delivery running.

ABC reports, and Coles' site confirms, that gift cards, Flybuys and Coles Plus services show no indication of impact. ABC also reports that customers of Woolworths, a separate company, reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions, and that Woolworths told ABC it was investigating; this is not part of Coles' disclosure.
sections.technical: Not disclosed by Coles. The ASX release and updates page give no attack type, vector, malware, CVE, affected systems or indicators of compromise. Coles has not named the experts or the ACSC engagement beyond the statement that it is working with them. No ATT&CK mapping is supported by the published material.
sections.guidance: Coles, on its updates page (not the ASX release): 'there is no action you need to take at this time'; it 'advise[s] everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend[s] remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information' and potential scam activity. In an updates-page FAQ, Coles recommends regularly updating passwords to a strong, unique password not reused across services. Coles says further updates will be given 'as appropriate' on its website. Liquorland's customer email, as quoted by The Shout, gives the customer response line 1800 061 562.
sections.differing:
Coles (ASX release, 16 Nov): no evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed; stores and online operating as normal.

ABC News: Coles 'has provided little detail' on what occurred, and told investors and customers it was business as usual.

iTnews: reports the same no-data-compromise wording from Coles' filing and that store and online operations are not affected.

shattered.io (analysis, not news reporting): notes that Coles has not said what kind of attack it faced or how the intruders got in, and that the filing covers customers, team members and suppliers but not other data categories. This is commentary, not a finding.
sections.unknown:
The cause, attack type and entry point. Whether any data was accessed, exfiltrated or encrypted; the investigation is ongoing and the no-evidence statement is limited to 'to date'. The number of affected Liquorland customers. The timing of intrusion and of detection. Whether there is a ransomware or leak-site claim (none is reported in the material read). Whether a regulator (OAIC, ACSC) has opened a separate inquiry. The identity of the 'global cyber security experts'. The reason for the Liquorland click-and-collect suspension and its end date.

**Label basis:** Coles' own ASX release (16 Nov 2026) confirms the incident and its no-data-compromise position; the scope and cause are not stated by Coles, and the Liquorland suspension rests on the Liquorland customer email as reported by The Shout.

items.headline: RIKEN takes Fugaku supercomputer offline after intrusion via operations-status dashboard; user names, emails, IDs and stored credentials may be exposed
items.summary: RIKEN says an external party entered Fugaku's internal operational network via a public status dashboard on 10–13 Nov 2026, tampered with servers, and may have taken user account data and stored credentials; Fugaku has been offline since 14 Nov.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
10–13 Nov 2026 (Japan time): an external third party used a publicly accessible web page showing Fugaku's operational status (a dashboard) to enter the internal operational network (RIKEN notice).
12 Nov: suspicious network traffic was detected; RIKEN then coordinated with the outsourced maintenance provider to begin an investigation (RIKEN notice).
13 Nov, 16:33 JST (07:33 UK): RIKEN confirmed unauthorised access. MEXT was notified at 20:59 JST the same day.
14 Nov, 04:30 JST (19:30 UK, 13 Nov): Fugaku operations suspended and the access route blocked. The affected system was isolated on 13 Nov at 22:07 JST and administrative keys replaced on 14 Nov at 20:20 JST.
15 Nov, 16:18 JST (07:18 UK): RIKEN emailed users. Per the Japanese notice, it also halted running and queued jobs; the English notice says RIKEN invalidated login public keys and asked users to revoke credentials stored on Fugaku.
16 Nov: RIKEN published its notice (the Japanese notice is dated 16 Nov 2026). The Personal Information Protection Commission was notified on 16 Nov at 17:55 JST.
17 Nov: Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the government and MEXT were investigating the cause and scope (Japan Times, reporting Tuesday's briefing).
sections.technical:
RIKEN: intrusion method not yet determined. The attacker moved from the public dashboard into the internal operational network, tampered with multiple internal servers, and installed malicious programs on some of them.
RIKEN: the attacker used some obtained credentials to try to connect to other systems; whether this caused further damage is under investigation.
No CVE, product version or IOC has been published by RIKEN. The Register's headline calls the dashboard a 'status page'; its text calls it a web dashboard. BleepingComputer calls it a public dashboard. RIKEN's text says only 'publicly accessible web page displaying Fugaku's operational status'.
sections.guidance:
RIKEN's notice asks users to revoke or remove the corresponding public key on each external service for any SSH private key stored on Fugaku and generate a new key pair, and to revoke and replace other stored credentials through the relevant service. It also says RIKEN will never ask for passwords by email and warns users to be wary of emails claiming to be from Fugaku or RIKEN.
RIKEN says it will resume operation only after measures to prevent recurrence, including addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing network configuration and implementing 'state-of-the-art security measures utilizing AI'.
sections.differing:
Japan Times: says RIKEN 'has not reported cases of accessed information being leaked yet'. RIKEN's notice says files and authentication-system information were 'either taken from the system or may have been taken', and that there is no concrete evidence research data left the system.
The Register: its headline refers to a 'status page hack' that exposed credentials, and its text says RIKEN knows that someone attempted to log onto Fugaku on 13 Nov. RIKEN's notice does not mention a 13 Nov login attempt.
BleepingComputer: says the malware 'targeted user data'. RIKEN says malicious programs were installed on some servers and does not describe their target.
User counts: RIKEN's English notice gives 'up to 4,222' Fugaku users in the text and 'up to 4,224' individuals in its table; the Japanese notice gives 4,222 Fugaku users (4,597 total including Rikyu). The Register and BleepingComputer use 4,222.
Japan Times: Kihara (government) says the cause and scope are being investigated; no government attribution has been made.
sections.unknown:
Intrusion method and the exploited software vulnerability (unnamed by RIKEN). Whether data outside Fugaku's authentication system was taken, and whether third-party personal data is in user files. Whether the stored credentials were used successfully on other systems: RIKEN says it is investigating this with the relevant agencies. Attacker identity and motive: no attribution by RIKEN or government. Date and terms of Fugaku's return to service. Whether the Rikyu system was affected beyond user-data exposure.

**Label basis:** RIKEN's own notices (English and Japanese, dated 16 Nov 2026) confirm unauthorised access, server tampering and possible data taking; intrusion method and full scope remain under investigation.

items.headline: Japan: PLAID KARTE platform breach exposes data at dozens of firms; Rakuten Securities test-environment leak up to 15.7M accounts; Rokkatei card skimming
items.summary: A third-party breach of PLAID's KARTE marketing platform has led dozens of Japanese firms (DHC, JINS, MUFG among them) to disclose customer data leaks, while Rakuten Securities said up to about 15.72M accounts may have leaked from a test environment holding unmasked production data and confectioner Rokkatei reported around 8,000 card records possibly skimmed from its checkout page.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
13 Nov 2026 (early morning, JST): PLAID detected unauthorised access to KARTE at 08:59 JST, disabled stolen credentials and began stopping servers from 14:27 JST, completing containment by about 15:23 JST; PLAID announced the incident on 13 Nov and paused all KARTE services.
16 Nov: PLAID published findings that the data affected included email addresses of 79,249 KARTE accounts, integration credentials (secret keys, access tokens) for external services, and member data some client companies had imported into KARTE; counts for the last two were still under investigation.
11-17 Nov onward: client companies began disclosing; JINS (17 Nov, per iThome) said up to about 18.29M member accounts may be affected and stopped data links on 13 Nov; DHC (18 Nov) confirmed about 19.11M customer records; MUFG (18 Nov, per iThome) confirmed about 6.5M customer records, without names, addresses or contact details.
17 Nov: Rakuten Securities apologised and said it had found unauthorised access to its systems on 16 Nov (ITmedia gives 16 Nov detection), after which it blocked access and made fixes. Rakuten says test-environment data may have leaked on 11 Nov.
18 Nov: Rokkatei (confectioner, Hokkaido) said its online shop checkout script was tampered with between 21 Oct 21:00 and 18 Nov 11:00 JST, and it took the shop offline; it reported the matter to the Personal Information Protection Commission.
18 Nov: ITmedia reports Rakuten Securities explained that production data was copied unmasked to a test server during an upgrade.
sections.technical:
PLAID (vendor notice, 16 Nov): attacker exploited a server vulnerability to steal database and system connection credentials, read data out of databases, then used the stolen credentials to take over a PLAID account and log into the admin interface. No CVE, CVSS or IOCs were published in the notices read.
Rakuten Securities (17 Nov): root cause and detailed circumstances remain under investigation; test environment held production customer data without masking, which the company said was for verification during an internal-system upgrade.
Rokkatei (18 Nov): payment-page program was tampered with so entered card data could be sent externally; the company says it does not store card data on its servers.
sections.guidance:
PLAID (16 Nov notice): asked customers whose KARTE integrations use external services to invalidate the linked credentials, and warned that phishing emails impersonating PLAID may be sent to KARTE account addresses.
Rakuten Securities (17 Nov notice): says over 90% of daily logins use passkeys and asks customers without passkeys to set them up; also points customers to a temporary-suspension setting for trading and withdrawals; says it does not send URLs in its emails and warns of impersonation emails, SMS, calls and post.
Rokkatei (18 Nov notice): asks cardholders who paid during the period to check statements; says it reported to the Personal Information Protection Commission.
DHC (per act1 article, 18 Nov): warned customers not to open links or attachments in emails impersonating DHC; says it is to file with the Personal Information Protection Commission jointly with PLAID.
sections.differing:
Rakuten Securities: says no leak of login passwords or PINs confirmed and no unauthorised trading confirmed linked to the incident.
Rakuten Securities (to ITmedia): says test environments normally hold only dummy data and the unmasked use was an exception following internal approval; it declined to say how long production data had been in test.
Social-media commentators (as reported by ITmedia) questioned the timing of the test copy relative to the intrusion and the notification method, which requires login; this is reported as commentary, not verified.
sections.unknown:
How many KARTE client companies are affected in total (dozens reported; PLAID counts still under investigation).
KARTE service restart date (PLAID: undetermined as of its 16 Nov notice).
Exact count of integration-credential records and imported member-data records at PLAID.
Whether the vulnerability exploited at PLAID is the same as, or related to, any other disclosed flaw; no CVE is published.
Whether any stolen data has been misused; DHC says no secondary harm has been confirmed, and Rakuten says no unauthorised trading linked to the incident has been confirmed.
Rokkatei: whether the tampering affected anything beyond the checkout script.

**Label basis:** PLAID, Rakuten Securities and Rokkatei published their own notices, which were read in full (PLAID 13 and 16 Nov, Rakuten 17 Nov, Rokkatei 18 Nov). DHC's figure is as reported by act1 and iThome (18–19 Nov); the JINS and MUFG figures are as reported by iThome. These are company-reported figures and are not verified against the companies' own notices.

items.headline: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline; about 265,000 customer accounts may have been compromised
items.summary: Transport for London says about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had account details compromised, which may include contact details, dates of birth and security question answers, and has taken the photocard website offline.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened:
Mon 16 Nov 2026: TfL says it became aware that Oyster photocard customers were receiving emails asking them to create an account they already had; the emails came from TfL's own systems (The Register).

Mon 16 Nov: TfL took the photocard website down while the activity was investigated (The Register; TfL statement via Britbrief).

Wed 18 Nov: TfL said around 265,000 photocard customers may have had account details compromised; it had contained the incident and contacted affected customers (TfL statement, via Britbrief and BBC-text copies; Britbrief timestamp 20:45 UK).

Thu 19 Nov: The Register reports the story (11:01 UK); the photocard website remains offline and no restoration date has been given (The Register).
sections.technical: TfL has not said how attackers got into its systems (The Register; BBC-text copy). No CVE, vendor or malware details were published in the material reviewed.
sections.guidance: TfL, as published: customers are asked to change their photocard account passwords and security questions and answers; if the same information is used elsewhere online, TfL says that should be changed too as a precaution (TfL statement via Britbrief). Customers who need to renew a photocard or query journey history are directed to TfL customer services on 0343 222 1234 (BBC-text copy; EuropeSays). Existing photocards still work at ticket barriers (The Register).
sections.differing:
TfL: no passwords, bank or payment card details, journey information, or names and dates of birth of Zip Oyster children were compromised; no evidence yet that the data has been used (TfL statement). TfL also says that, because of the speed with which the incident was identified and addressed, 'the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced' (TfL statement via Britbrief).

The Register notes TfL has been more specific about what was not taken than what was. The Register says TfL notified more than 7 million customers after its September 2024 cyberattack, and that about 5,000 were contacted as a priority because bank account details may have been compromised. BBC reporting later said the data of about 10 million people had been stolen in that 2024 attack (BBC-text copy). The Register says there is nothing to suggest the two incidents are related.
sections.unknown:
How attackers gained access. Whether any data has been misused. When the photocard website will be restored. Whether the ICO will take action on this incident: TfL says it has notified the ICO, and the ICO took no enforcement action over the 2024 incident, deeming TfL's response proportionate (The Register). Whether the 'around 265,000' figure may change, since TfL uses 'may have'. No attacker claim or ICO statement on this incident was reported in the material reviewed.

**Label basis:** Operator's own statement (TfL director Shashi Verma, quoted in The Register and in matching text in BBC-text copies); TfL says it notified the ICO. No attacker claim or ICO statement was found.
