items.headline: Wellington IT breach exposes saved payee data at around 40 Irish credit unions
items.summary: Belfast-based banking software supplier Wellington IT confirmed a cyber security incident affecting its CU Online platform; saved payee records (names, IBANs, BICs, account numbers, references) at around 40 Irish credit unions may have been accessed; the company says it has taken steps to address the issue, and regulators are assessing breach notifications.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened: Early October 2026: per Wellington IT's correspondence to credit unions (as quoted by the Irish Examiner and BleepingComputer), an automated script made requests against an authorisation flaw on the CU Online platform between 2 and 4 October; the flaw was reportedly fixed on 6 October (per Cavan Credit Union notice as reported by iThome). Irish Times and Silicon Republic give 6 October as the exploitation date, differing from the 2–4 October window. 16 Nov (Mon): Wellington IT emailed affected credit unions warning of a potential breach; Irish Examiner reports that WIT had been told by a credit union the previous Friday that extortion emails had been sent to it and several credit unions. 17 Nov (Tue): credit unions began notifying the DPC; Central Bank said some had notified it; Department of Finance called it a 'possible cybersecurity incident' affecting 'a limited number of credit unions'. 18 Nov (Wed): Minister Robert Troy said the delay was 'not acceptable' and that he had written to Wellington IT seeking a meeting; credit unions began informing members. 19 Nov (Thu): Wellington IT CEO Colin Mitchell issued a statement (via BleepingComputer and RTÉ). Times are UK time where known; reporting timestamps are not given in all sources.
sections.technical: Authorisation flaw in the CU Online digital/mobile banking platform (per Wellington IT correspondence quoted by Irish Examiner and Silicon Republic). Attack described as an automated script making requests; figures differ (see differing). Payee data at risk: payee names, nicknames, bank names, IBANs, BICs, account numbers, sort codes, addresses, payment references. Logs needed to identify which records were retrieved are not available per WIT. No CVE, CVSS or IOCs have been published. Wellington IT's statement does not mention a CVE.
sections.guidance: Central Bank of Ireland (via RTÉ, 17-18 Nov): members should contact their credit union with concerns; it expects credit unions to inform potentially affected members without undue delay. Central Bank (via RTÉ): members should be wary of unexpected calls, texts or emails about credit union accounts or payments, and should never transfer money because of an unexpected call, text or email. Irish League of Credit Unions statement (via RTÉ and Irish Times): understands the vulnerability is closed and member accounts and balances were not compromised. Credit union notices (as reported by BleepingComputer, not attributed to WIT or any authority): members should remain vigilant for phishing and impersonation attempts.
sections.differing: Wellington IT (CEO statement, 19 Nov): it 'alerted its customers as soon as the potential risk to customer data was confirmed'; it has 'engaged external cybersecurity experts'; investigation ongoing; collaborating with the DPC, NCSC and GNCCB. Minister of State Robert Troy (RTÉ, 18 Nov): the delay by the provider in informing credit unions is 'not acceptable'; he has sought a meeting. Tánaiste Simon Harris called the suspected breach 'deeply concerning' (Irish Times, 17 Nov). Wellington IT in its earlier correspondence (per Irish Times, Silicon Republic): 1.4 million malicious requests; per Irish Examiner: five million requests. BleepingComputer: the attacker accessed private records 'using valid credentials' (BleepingComputer's own wording, citing notices it says it saw; not confirmed by WIT); Irish Examiner and Silicon Republic describe an authorisation flaw. Number of credit unions: 'around 40' (Troy, RTÉ); more than 40 (Irish Times, 17 Nov); 'approximately 50' (St Canice's, Leinster Express); 'about 50 credit unions, 43 in Ireland' (BleepingComputer, Irish Examiner). Irish credit union count: 160 (TheJournal, Troy), 172 (RTÉ), 184 registered (TheJournal citing Central Bank). Department of Finance: 'limited number'. Minister of State Troy: no financial loss has been experienced by any credit union or its members (RTÉ, 18 Nov); ILCU and credit unions: member accounts and balances not compromised.
sections.unknown:
Total number of individuals affected (Wellington IT said it would provide figures 'as soon as possible'). Which individual payee records were retrieved (WIT says logs are unavailable). Whether any fraud has followed. Who is responsible for the attack and whether data has been published or sold; the extortion emails' contents and sender are not described in any source read. The full list of affected credit unions (credit union notices cited by iThome include North East, Cavan and Ballincollig Credit Union; not verified against the notices). The DPC's position and any formal regulatory action. The outcome of the Minister's meeting with Wellington IT. Why the flaw was not disclosed until mid-November.

**Label basis:** Wellington IT CEO Colin Mitchell's statement (quoted in full by BleepingComputer, updated 19/11, and paraphrased by RTÉ and TheJournal) confirms a cyber security incident; the DPC confirmed receipt of breach notifications. The number affected and the exact data scope are not confirmed by the company.

items.headline: India: alleged PayU cloud payout fraud (Rs 25.67 crore) and NBFC loan diversions (over Rs 65 crore) per police; CERT-In flags e-Sushrut HMIS flaws; CreditNirvana (Perfios) flaws exposed 6.6 million accounts
items.summary: Gurugram police say attackers used PayU cloud servers to move Rs 25.67 crore (two men arrested); Delhi Police describe NBFC loan diversions over Rs 65 crore; CERT-In rated four e-Sushrut HMIS flaws high severity on 17 Nov; a researcher disclosed CreditNirvana (Perfios) flaws exposing 6.6 million accounts, which the researcher says were fixed in June.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM

sections.happened:
**17 Nov 2026:** CERT-In issued vulnerability note CIVN-2026-0557 rating several flaws in C-DAC's e-Sushrut HMIS as high severity (Original Issue Date 17 Nov per CERT-In).

**26 Oct 2026:** CERT-In issued vulnerability note CIVN-2026-0523 for the CreditNirvana flaws, per the researcher's write-up.

**9 Oct 2026:** CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin advisory CIAD-2026-0046 warned NBFCs, lenders, fintechs and payment providers about attackers abusing payment and disbursement APIs.

**5 Nov 2026 (about 11:30 pm):** PayU's security team detected unusual payout-API activity, according to MediaNama citing Hindustan Times; transfers had already occurred.

**9 Nov 2026:** PayU Payments Pvt Ltd filed a complaint with Gurugram Cyber Police (police statement, as reported by PTI and The420.in).

**15 Nov 2026:** Gurugram Cyber Police arrested two men in Ludhiana, allegedly for supplying bank accounts (police statement).

**16 Nov 2026:** Delhi Police describe approved but undisbursed NBFC loans diverted at 12 NBFCs in Delhi-NCR over three months, over Rs 65 crore; police say these cases are part of over 150 FIRs filed by NBFCs across India (per the Indian Express, as reported by MediaNama and The420.in).

**16-17 Nov 2026:** The Economic Times, as summarised by Business Today (17 Nov, 4:12 pm IST), reports NPCI has approached Google about operating-system safeguards against UPI fraud involving sideloaded malicious apps.

**18 Nov 2026:** WIRED, the researcher's write-up and Indian outlets report the CreditNirvana disclosure. The researcher says Perfios fixed both flaws on 2 June 2026.
sections.technical:
**e-Sushrut HMIS (C-DAC Noida), per CERT-In CIVN-2026-0557:**
- Insufficient authentication and session validation in the dashboard functionality (CVE-2026-124643): unauthenticated crafted HTTP requests can reach hospital dashboard information.
- Internal operational statistics embedded in the login-page HTML (CVE-2026-124644), extractable without credentials.
- Static, predictable client-side password-hashing value on the login page (CVE-2026-124645); OpenCVE rates it CVSS 4.0 8.7 and classifies it as CWE-321.
- Insecure direct object reference in an API endpoint (CVE-2026-124646): CERT-In says an unauthenticated attacker could enumerate patient information; Strix rates it CVSS 8.7 (CVSS 4.0 vector AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N).
- CERT-In note CIVN-2026-0207 (28 Apr 2026) rated five earlier e-Sushrut CVEs (CVE-2026-42513 to 42517) critical, per MediaNama.

**CreditNirvana (Perfios), per researcher Eaton Zveare's write-up:**
- Hardcoded API key in client-side JavaScript giving access to the Agentic AI Call Center (CVE-2026-110474, 8.7 High per the write-up; CERT-In rated it high).
- Improper authentication in the primary collections platform allowing login as an administrator (CVE-2026-110475, 9.3 Critical per the write-up; CERT-In rated it critical).
- Clients named in reporting: Aditya Birla Capital Finance, BharatPe and International Asset Reconstruction Company.

**Payment-fraud pattern, per CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin CIAD-2026-0046:** stolen payment-gateway and partner-bank API credentials used to call disbursal APIs from whitelisted infrastructure, bypassing loan, KYC and limit controls; hard-coded or plaintext long-lived tokens; exposed deprecated APIs; attacker IPs mainly hosting infrastructure; possible AI-assisted tooling.

**Police account of NBFC attacks (as reported):** malware on customer-facing applications, dwell time of 7-8 days, beneficiary bank details replaced with mule accounts, and instructions sent from cloud-server IPs already trusted by the NBFC's firewall. Police say a platform named CyberStrikeAI was allegedly used in one October incident of about Rs 3 crore.
sections.guidance:
- **CERT-In (CIVN-2026-0557):** contact C-DAC for upgrading e-Sushrut HMIS to the latest version.
- **CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin (CIAD-2026-0046):** entities are advised to report any signs of suspicious activity related to the campaign to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin.
- **Delhi Police (as reported by The420.in):** have advised NBFCs to strengthen cybersecurity controls, conduct system audits and follow CERT-In recommendations.
sections.differing:
- **PayU / police:** Gurugram police say attackers accessed three cloud servers, manipulated the payout API and made 265 unauthorised transactions to 156 bank accounts; the two arrested men allegedly supplied accounts for a 2% commission. PayU has made no public statement found in the sources read.
- **Perfios / CreditNirvana:** did not respond to WIRED's requests for comment. The researcher's write-up says the flaws were fixed on 2 June. Neither the write-up nor WIRED says anyone other than the researcher accessed the data.
- **RBI:** MediaNama, citing Head & Tales, says RBI issued a confidential advisory on AI-assisted attacks earlier in November and another on API hijacking on 16 Nov; not verified.
- **NPCI / Google:** as summarised by Business Today, the ET report cites people in the know in the payments industry; no NPCI or Google public statement found.
sections.unknown:
- How the PayU attackers got into the three cloud servers (police audit pending, per reports); whether the CERT-In CIAD-2026-0046 vulnerabilities were involved.
- Total losses at the 12 NBFCs and the other FIRs; how much of the Rs 65 crore is recovered.
- Whether any e-Sushrut deployments were exploited; the number of affected hospitals and patients.
- Whether the CreditNirvana data was accessed by anyone beyond the researcher.
- Whether NPCI and Google will agree any operating-system measures.
- Status of the PayU complaint and any company statement.

**Label basis:** UNCONFIRMED CLAIM for the item as a whole. The CERT-In vulnerability notes are official publications, and CERT-In note CIVN-2026-0523 is cited in the researcher's write-up and in WIRED coverage (not opened), and the CreditNirvana CVEs and severities rest on that write-up and those reports; the PayU and NBFC incidents, arrests, loss figures and AI attribution rest on police statements as reported by outlets, and PayU has made no public statement.

items.headline: Ethiopian Airlines warns ShebaMiles members of possible data exposure from 'limited scope' cyber incident, a week after Air Botswana's suspected-ransomware disclosure
items.summary: Ethiopian Airlines emailed ShebaMiles members on 18 Nov 2026 that a cybersecurity incident of limited scope may have exposed some customer information, with no evidence financial data was accessed; no intrusion date, data categories or victim count given.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED

sections.happened:
Air Botswana (state-owned) detected unauthorised access on 3 Nov 2026 to systems holding employee and internal information, described it as suspected ransomware, and posted a public notice on 4 Nov saying passenger booking, aircraft, flight operations and aviation safety systems were unaffected (3News; TechCabal gives the same description without the notice date). The Air Botswana notice itself was not retrieved for this brief.

On Wed 18 Nov 2026 Ethiopian Airlines sent a notice to ShebaMiles members (TechCabal, published 15:07 UK; Capital Newspaper; 3News). Reuters reported on 19 Nov (09:24 UK) that CEO Mesfin Tasew told Reuters late on 18 Nov the investigation was under way but gave no detail.

Reuters reported that Ethiopian Airlines flights were not disrupted. The notice itself, per TechCabal and 3News, did not address bookings or flight operations.
sections.technical: None published. No CVE, ATT&CK technique, IOC, threat-actor attribution or root cause has been disclosed by Ethiopian Airlines or Air Botswana. No ransomware group has been reported as claiming either incident in the sources read.
sections.differing:
Ethiopian Airlines: incident 'of limited scope' that 'recently occurred'; 'may have affected certain customer information'; 'currently no evidence' that financial information was accessed; investigating with cybersecurity partners and relevant authorities (airline notice, quoted in part by Reuters and Capital Newspaper).

TechCabal and 3News note the notice gave no date, no data categories, no victim count and no statement on whether bookings or flight operations were affected; 3News says it gave no password-reset guidance. These are reporters' observations, not airline claims.

TechCabal and 3News describe Air Botswana's ransomware label as 'suspected'; Air Botswana has not said whether data was copied (TechCabal).
sections.unknown:
Date of the Ethiopian intrusion; which systems and data categories were involved; number of ShebaMiles members affected (membership cited as 5.38m+ in 2025, not an affected count); whether bookings or operations were touched; whether any group has claimed the incident; whether either airline has notified Ethiopia's or Botswana's data regulator.

Relationship between the two incidents: no source reports a shared vendor, actor or technique. TechCabal's 'a week after' is a timing comparison only. Not established either way.

The Ethiopian Airlines notice and the Air Botswana notice were not retrievable for this brief on the airlines' own sites; both are known only through press quotation.

**Label basis:** Rests on the airline's own customer notice (quoted in part by Reuters and Capital Newspaper) and its CEO's confirmation to Reuters that an investigation is under way; details are thin, hence VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED rather than CONFIRMED.

items.headline: Banco do Brasil confirms unauthorised access to customer personal data via a valid credential; TJMG confirms leaked files after a cyber incident
items.summary: Banco do Brasil says a third party used a valid credential to access customers' personal data (name, CPF, email, branch, sometimes account number) on 12 Nov; the Tribunal de Justiça de Minas Gerais (TJMG) confirms files were leaked after a cyber incident and that ANPD and police were notified.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened:
13 Nov 2026 (Fri): TJMG publishes its first note on a cybersecurity incident identified in recent days, saying no judicial or administrative system was compromised or accessed (TJMG portal, 'TJMG identifica incidente de segurança cibernético', 11h54 Brasília time).
14 Nov 2026 (Sat): TJMG says it verified that some leaked files had been published; says technical analyses confirm the judicial and administrative systems were not compromised and database integrity was preserved, preventive blocking and password resets were applied, potentially affected data subjects are being contacted individually, and ANPD and police were notified (TJMG portal update of 14 Nov, 18h06 Brasília time; Itatiaia, CNN Brasil, Jornal de Brasília and O Tempo carry the same note).
12 Nov 2026: Banco do Brasil identifies unauthorised access to customers' personal data (per the bank's notice).
18 Nov 2026 (Wed): Banco do Brasil sends a notice to account holders disclosing the access; ConvergenciaDigital published first (20:34 UK), followed by Mixvale, Exame, CNN Brasil and SBT News. Outlets differ on the weekday ('quinta-feira (18)' in ConvergenciaDigital, SBT and Exame; 'quarta-feira (18)' in Mixvale); 18 Nov 2026 is a Wednesday.
sections.technical:
Banco do Brasil (notice as reported): unauthorised access by third parties using a valid credential; the credential has been revoked. The bank says its systems were not breached, that no passwords, tokens, security codes or authentication mechanisms were exposed, and that no financial transactions resulting from the incident were identified. No ATT&CK mapping, CVE or IOCs were published by either organisation.
TJMG: no CVE, vendor or IOC published; states its judicial and administrative systems were not compromised and database integrity was preserved.
sections.guidance:
Banco do Brasil (as reported): customers are told the bank will never ask for passwords, security codes, app installation or transfers to supposedly safe accounts, and to be alert to suspicious messages and contacts.
TJMG (as reported): affected people are contacted individually for guidance on account security; the court refers questions to its 'Fale com o TJMG' channel.
sections.differing:
Banco do Brasil (notice as quoted by CNN Brasil): "Não houve invasão aos sistemas, exposição de senhas, tokens ou códigos de segurança, nem foram identificadas transações financeiras decorrentes do incidente". The same notice, as reported by Exame, SBT News, CNN Brasil and Mixvale, says the main risk from the exposed identification and contact data is fraud attempts using phishing and social engineering that impersonate the bank.
TJMG: no judicial or administrative system was compromised (the court's account, carried by Itatiaia and O Tempo as its position). Neither organisation's statements have been independently verified.
sections.unknown:
How the valid credential was obtained and whose credential it was (Mixvale notes the notice does not say); which actor(s) are responsible; how many customers (Banco do Brasil) and how many files and people (TJMG) are affected; what the leaked TJMG files contain; whether the two incidents are related (no source links them).

**Label basis:** Both organisations' own statements. TJMG's portal notices of 13 and 14 Nov were read directly. Banco do Brasil's customer notice was not available from the bank's own site and was read as reproduced by five outlets (ConvergenciaDigital, SBT News, Exame, CNN Brasil, Mixvale), which report the same details consistently.

items.headline: Leaked Deutsche Bank files (more than 15M records, "Inside Deutsche Bank") allege dealings with Russian oligarchs and sanctions-linked clients; Hesse data protection authority opens probe
items.summary: A consortium of more than 200 journalists published "Inside Deutsche Bank" on 17 Nov 2026, based on more than 15 million internal records from two whistleblowers (The Insider: 15.6M); the bank says its IT is not indicated as compromised and it has informed authorities, while the Hesse data protection commissioner has opened an investigation.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.firstReported: 17 Nov, morning (before Frankfurt trading moved; exact time not verified)

sections.happened:
**17 Nov 2026.** The "Inside Deutsche Bank" investigation (Barracuda Media / Project Barracuda) was published by a consortium of international journalists, with outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde (Reuters). Deutsche Bank shares fell by as much as 6% in Frankfurt trade (Reuters) and were 4.7% lower by 9:20am ET (CNBC). The Insider's English article is timestamped 17:52 UK time.

Scale and sourcing: Reuters (via onvista, translated from German) reports 15 million documents including more than nine million emails; Euronews, Al Jazeera and Himal say more than 15 million; The Insider says 15.6 million. Journalist counts differ: more than 200 (CNBC, Himal) or more than 230 from about 50 outlets (The Insider, Al Jazeera). Journalists Josy Joseph and Khadija Sharife obtained the cache from two whistleblowers (Al Jazeera, Himal).

Reported content (claims by the consortium and its partners, not verified): dealings with Russian oligarchs and companies tied to sanctioned owners (Reuters and Al Jazeera describe business pursued up to the February 2022 invasion; The Insider's headline says the bank served Russian companies after 2022); about $582M in Epstein-linked suspicious transactions; and an inadvertent 2017 disclosure of Donald Trump's tax document to another client's accountant (FT, via CNBC, Al Jazeera and Reuters).

Same day: Deutsche Bank published a statement on the reporting (db.com, 17 Nov). Chairman Alexander Wynaendts backed CEO Christian Sewing in an emailed statement (Reuters). Trump, asked in Manila about the 2017 tax-document incident, said the bank should not have disclosed it: "It's illegal for them to do it" (Reuters, Al Jazeera); the bank declined to comment. German finance minister Lars Klingbeil called on authorities to investigate and the bank to explain how it fixed failures (Reuters).

**18 Nov.** The Hesse data protection commissioner, Alexander Roßnagel, told Handelsblatt (via Reuters/onvista and HASEPOST, both translated from German) that he has opened an investigation under the GDPR. He is examining whether the bank had appropriate technical and organisational measures, whether it reported the incident in time (the GDPR 72-hour rule is cited in the reports) and whether it promptly notified affected persons; the authority has asked for further documents and he declined to comment on possible sanctions. Euronews says the probe does not assess the content of the documents. Sewing told Handelsblatt that "looking back, you can always say that at a certain point in time you might have been able to prioritise differently" (Euronews).

**19 Nov.** Reuters (via TradingView, snippet only) reports Sewing said clients were calm and the bank was not seeing an impact on its business.
sections.technical: No technical vulnerability, attack vector or IOCs have been published. The bank states that, after testing with a security firm, there is no indication its current IT environment is compromised and that no account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed. The source of the leak is described only as two whistleblowers who copied the files (Al Jazeera, Himal). Their lawyer says they also passed material to the US Department of Justice, FinCEN and HMRC (Himal); Al Jazeera says to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities.
sections.guidance: Deutsche Bank (statement, 17 Nov): it has informed the relevant authorities, including the data protection authority, and has proactively contacted clients or colleagues it knows may be materially affected. Hesse data protection commissioner (Handelsblatt interview, via Reuters): an investigation is under way into technical and organisational measures and the timing and content of notifications; no outcome published.
sections.differing:
**Deutsche Bank** (statement, 17 Nov): the documents are "purported" and "allegedly disclosed"; the matters date back many years, in some cases two decades; the bank reviewed them at the time and worked with regulators; it has invested EUR 7bn in controls (2019–2025). CNBC and Al Jazeera quote the bank as saying it is "a different bank today"; Al Jazeera reports the bank said it did not expect any meaningful financial impact.

**Consortium:** the files show repeated missed warnings on money laundering and sanctions and that the bank bent its own rules for powerful clients (Himal, The Insider). **Timing of the Russia dealings:** The Insider's headline says the bank served Russian companies and transacted for sanctioned oligarchs after 2022, while Reuters and Al Jazeera describe business up to the February 2022 invasion.

**Trump:** the bank's 2017 disclosure of his tax information was illegal (Reuters, Al Jazeera). **Whistleblowers:** they said they believed the files contained indications of potential criminal misconduct (Himal).
sections.unknown:
Whether the bank's statement of "no indication" of compromise will be backed by a published forensic finding. Whether the Hesse authority will find a reporting or notification failure. Authenticity of individual documents has not been independently verified in the sources reviewed. Scope of the data subjects affected and whether individuals have been notified. Whether US or UK authorities will act on the material given to them. When, within 17 Nov, the first reports were published. The Reuters report of 19 Nov was available only as a snippet and was not read in full for this brief.

**Label basis:** Deutsche Bank's own statement (17 Nov) acknowledges purported internal documents including confidential client data and says it informed authorities, and a data protection regulator has opened a probe; the specific allegations about Russian clients and others are reporters' claims, not verified.

items.headline: AfD email leak: Correctiv reports donation questions, far-right contacts and back-room circles in leaked mail
items.summary: Correctiv (17 Nov 2026) reports on hundreds of thousands of leaked AfD emails and documents, citing possible earlier knowledge by Alice Weidel of a 2017 Swiss donation, far-right links and back-room discussion circles; the AfD confirmed the hack but says it will not answer questions on the contents, and Weidel's spokesperson has disputed the donation account.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.firstReported: 17 Nov 05:01 (Correctiv overview); the leak itself was first reported on 20 Oct

sections.happened:
September 2026: the AfD says a hosting provider used by the party was attacked and that parts of a few mailboxes, most unused for years, were copied unlawfully (AfD statement quoted by ZDF; Euronews/AFP quotes a similar AfD statement).

Mon 19 Oct 2026: according to Correctiv's 21 Oct article, a hacker group calling itself Hexane published about 420,000 emails, many with attachments. Correctiv's 17 Nov overview describes the publication more loosely as 'end of October'.

Tue 20 Oct 2026: the AfD confirms the attack and says users were informed (Euronews, citing AFP). Bild reports more than 421,000 emails taken, including messages of Alice Weidel and Alexander Gauland. Euronews says a website published what it said were summaries of some emails, not the originals, and that it was unclear who was responsible and whether more data was taken.

21 Oct 2026: ZDFheute explainer: more than 420,000 emails and over 50,000 attached documents; dataset about 300 GB; the AfD says it has filed a criminal complaint over the attack and publication, though Berlin prosecutors had not yet confirmed receipt (ZDF).

23 Oct 2026: ZDF, Der Standard and Spiegel report on emails relating to the 2017 Swiss donation to Weidel's district association; Weidel's spokesperson responds (ZDF).

17 Nov 2026 (05:01 UK time): Correctiv publishes an overview ('Was steckt wirklich im AfD-Leak') and a feature on AfD-linked discussion circles ('Die Hinterzimmer der extremen Rechten'). Correctiv says its team verifies the data itself and checks each piece of information it publishes on, and that DKIM signatures are included in only part of the data, so verification by that route is limited. Correctiv describes the release as two levels: AI-categorised summaries on a homepage, and a 281 GB archive offered as a torrent (the link is not reproduced here).

Correctiv's main reported points: a 132,000 euro split donation from Switzerland in July-Sept 2017 to Weidel's district association, for which the party later paid a penalty of nearly 400,000 euros; a 2017 NRW campaign newspaper ('Extrablatt') funded via an association behind which Correctiv says stood the Swiss agency Goal AG; a ZDF investigation, cited by Correctiv, reporting that in 2018 staff of AfD MP Markus Frohnmaier forwarded documents marked 'Verschlusssache – Nur für den Dienstgebrauch' to his private email address; and, for the Bonn 'Godesberger Pressestammtisch', invitation emails since 2013 from which Correctiv identified more than 170 invitees.

Personal-data aspects reported by Correctiv: it cites Tagesspiegel for personal data of about 8,700 party donors in the leak; Zeit and Handelsblatt for at least 23,000 first-time voters in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern affected (data the party had requested from registration offices); and its own finding that press-ID data of at least 1,000 journalists had been publicly retrievable on the AfD website. The Berlin data protection authority and the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state data protection commissioner have opened review proceedings (Correctiv). The contents of that personal data are not reproduced here.
sections.technical:
Attack vector as described by the AfD: compromise of a hosting provider used by the party. No CVE, vulnerability or IOC has been published by the AfD or any authority in the sources read. Group name per Correctiv: Hexane (unverified beyond Correctiv). Dataset: 281 GB (Correctiv) or about 300 GB (ZDF). Emails: about 420,000 (Correctiv, ZDF) or more than 421,000 (Bild via Euronews). Documents: about 49,000 (Correctiv) or over 50,000 (ZDF). Correctiv says the emails run from March 2013 to September 2026.

Verification method described by Correctiv: metadata analysis, comparison of documents and timing, use of public registers, and DKIM signatures where present (not available for all data). ZDF says many emails carry a digital signature that can be matched for authenticity. Correctiv says the author of a 2021 email confirmed its authenticity to it; other authenticity claims are not independently confirmed.
sections.differing:
AfD: parts of 'a few mailboxes, most unused for years' were copied unlawfully, the attack was quickly detected and stopped and users were informed (AfD statement via Euronews/AFP and ZDF); ZDF also quotes the party saying large data volumes flowed out. The party says it will not answer questions about the content (Correctiv). Correctiv, citing Zeit and Handelsblatt, says the AfD first rejected responsibility for the insecure transmission of first-time voters' data and pointed to the registration offices that sent it unencrypted.

Correctiv and ZDF: hundreds of thousands of emails and tens of thousands of documents, including mailboxes of Weidel, Gauland and (per ZDF) Leif-Erik Holm; ZDF says classified government and Bundestag committee documents are included.

Weidel donation: Correctiv says the emails suggest Weidel could have known of the Swiss payments earlier than she has publicly admitted (she has said she learned of the donation in September 2017), and cites NDR, WDR and Spiegel research that she was more closely involved in handling the payments than previously known. ZDF (23 Oct) reports emails of July 2017 in which Weidel asked for a separate account for donations; Weidel's spokesperson said she had held many conversations with potential supporters, that the sub-account was set up for that reason, and that she neither expected specific sums nor was sure individuals would donate. ZDF also notes the Konstanz prosecutor earlier closed an investigation of Weidel for lack of sufficient suspicion, and that the Bundestag administration regards the donation as an inadmissible straw-donor donation.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig (SPD), as reported by Correctiv: she wants to use the mails for examining a possible AfD ban procedure if they provide evidence of unconstitutional aims (not checked against a primary statement).
sections.unknown:
Who carried out the hack and the publication beyond the group name Hexane given by Correctiv; whether more data was taken than the mailboxes the AfD named; the authenticity of individual documents beyond what Correctiv, ZDF and others have checked; whether Weidel's account of the 2017 donation is accurate; what the Bundestag administration and the Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern data protection authorities will decide; whether the Federal Ministry of Justice will open any proceedings based on the material; the outcome of the AfD's criminal complaint. Correctiv says most people it approached for the Hinterzimmer piece did not reply. The NDR/WDR, Spiegel, Zeit and Handelsblatt reports cited by Correctiv were not read directly for this brief; they are known only as quoted by Correctiv or in search excerpts.

**Label basis:** CONFIRMED for the incident: the AfD itself confirmed the hack and the unlawful copying of mailboxes and said large data volumes flowed out (AfD statements via ZDF and Euronews/AFP), and ZDF, Correctiv and Euronews/AFP report it independently. The content claims in Correctiv's reporting are attributed to Correctiv's own document review and remain unconfirmed by the AfD.

items.headline: Ransomware gangs The Gentlemen and n0n claim data theft from Nvidia, Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan; companies respond
items.summary: The Gentlemen listed Nvidia on its leak site with a countdown to 28 Nov; Nvidia says it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner and has found no indication its own systems or networks were affected. The n0n group listed 59 organisations as victims and claims data from several, including Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan; Visa says the incident originated with a third-party provider in Asia-Pacific, and JPMorgan says a software bug, not an attack, caused its 16 Nov outage. n0n has since published datasets labelled Mastercard and JPMorgan, whose authenticity and origin are unverified; The Gentlemen has published no files for Nvidia.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM

sections.happened:
16 Nov (UK time not visible): The n0n group's leak site named 59 organisations, including Visa, Mastercard, JPMorgan Chase, Eli Lilly, Walmart and P&G (iThome; Daily Security Review). Daily Security Review, citing RansomNews, says 46 of the entries had been numbered placeholders since 9 Nov and were replaced with company names on 16 Nov.

16 Nov: JPMorgan Chase reported a 'temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems' affecting some consumer transactions (CNBC). A JPMorgan spokesperson told CNBC 'There is no evidence it is cyber-related.'

17 Nov: per Daily Security Review and Cybernews, n0n listed Visa and JPMorgan with a 48-hour countdown to publication.

18 Nov (Wednesday): per Newsweek, The Gentlemen added Nvidia to its dark web leak site with a countdown; Newsweek says the listing had Nvidia's logo, ticker and revenue, a Tox contact and no sample files. Cybernews's first article on the listing was published at 12:38 UK.

19 Nov, 07:25 UK: Cybernews updated its Nvidia article with Nvidia's statement. 09:23 UK (04:23 EST): BleepingComputer reported Nvidia's response (see differing); it says the countdown ends on 28 Nov.

19 Nov, 10:02 and 10:22 UK: after the 48-hour deadline, Cybernews reported that n0n had published datasets labelled Mastercard (about 280KB, roughly 2,000 entries) and JPMorgan (about 502KB).
sections.differing:
The Gentlemen (per the leak-site listing, as reported by BleepingComputer, Cybernews and Newsweek): claims it has stolen Nvidia data and threatens publication if negotiations fail. The listing gives no further detail and no files.

Nvidia (spokesperson, to BleepingComputer and Cybernews): 'NVIDIA is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. We have found no indication that NVIDIA systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation.' Newsweek reports Nvidia has not publicly confirmed a breach.

n0n (per Cybernews and iThome): claims customer data from Visa (Asia-Pacific marketing interactions), Mastercard (Middle East and Africa) and JPMorgan (Reserve-programme-related data and member directories). Daily Security Review reports that Bitdefender found encryptor code on an exposed server and assessed that n0n had hit just over 20 victims, well below the number on its leak site.

Published data (Cybernews, 19 Nov): after the deadline n0n published about 2,000 entries (280KB) attributed to Mastercard, which Cybernews's researcher says is likely test data, and about 502KB attributed to JPMorgan (Cybernews counts roughly 16,000 customer email addresses). Cybernews says authenticity and origin are not independently verified and reports no published Visa dataset.

Visa (to Cybernews): aware of the claims; Cybernews says Visa told it the incident originated with a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region. Visa said: 'Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted. There is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected.' Visa has not named the provider.

JPMorgan (to CNBC and Cybernews): 'no evidence' the 16 Nov outage was cyber-related; attributed it to a software bug in on-premise hardware. JPMorgan had not commented on the n0n claims at the time of Cybernews's 19 Nov article.

Mastercard: Cybernews says it contacted Mastercard for comment; no response is reported in the article.

Cybernews researcher Aras Nazarovas: the Mastercard, Visa and JPMorgan datasets appear to come from one third-party source, not the institutions' own systems; he also says The Gentlemen has previously exaggerated claims and misattributed victims.
sections.unknown:
Whether Nvidia data was taken at all, and from which unit or partner; neither Nvidia's partner nor Visa's provider has been named. The authenticity and origin of the n0n Mastercard and JPMorgan datasets are unverified, and no Visa dataset has been reported. Whether the JPMorgan outage and the n0n claims are related (JPMorgan has said there is no evidence of a cyberattack). Mastercard's response. Whether the n0n list of 59 names is accurate. The leak timelines and date of intrusion. No Nvidia-published statement was read for this brief; the statement is as given to BleepingComputer and Cybernews.

**Label basis:** The Gentlemen's Nvidia claim rests on a leak-site listing with no files or evidence. n0n has published datasets labelled Mastercard and JPMorgan, but their authenticity and origin are unverified and Cybernews's researcher says they appear to come from one third party. Company responses (Nvidia, Visa, JPMorgan) address their own systems or a partner incident and do not verify any claim.

items.headline: Optimizely Web Experimentation hijacked to serve card-skimming, crypto-clipping and iOS exploit-kit JavaScript on 178 organisations' sites
items.summary: On 16 Nov an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation signup flow to write malicious code into customers' Project JavaScript; Report URI found it in 188 snippets across 178 organisations (incl. BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, GitLab, IKEA), and Optimizely has confirmed the incident, closed the flaw and cleaned the code.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened:
All times UTC (= UK time on these dates) unless stated.

**16 Nov 2026.** Per Optimizely's customer incident report, the attacker created the first account via the Web Experimentation signup flow at 00:37 and Optimizely says the first malicious code was written to a customer project at 07:51. Report URI's own timeline records the first injected Optimizely snippet (a BBC snippet loading code from `webshell.lol`) at 04:21; the main payload `track.js` was first built at 08:10 and seen on bbc.com at 08:28. Scott Helme (Report URI) says Report URI's threat-intelligence pipeline first flagged the activity on a customer site at 15:06. Optimizely says it detected the activity at 13:34, blocked malicious outbound code at Cloudflare at 16:06, closed the flaw at 16:10, ended sessions and revoked tokens at 16:53, and removed the injected code from all affected projects by 22:24. Report URI observed mass clean-up from about 20:40 to 21:10; one snippet (TalkTalk, per IBTimes UK and StepSecurity citing The Register) was still infected at 21:52 and all were clean by 23:11. Report URI published its findings at 22:47.

**17 Nov.** Optimizely posted a status-page notice at 01:02 and issued statements to media; Optimizely's incident report to customers is dated 17 Nov (Krebs added a link to it on 18 Nov). The registry put the payload domain `1688360.cc` on clientHold at 00:37 and `webshell.lol` at 03:37 (Report URI). The attacker's wallets were emptied 04:11–05:39 (Report URI, StepSecurity); Report URI also records an earlier sweep of stablecoins at 13:03–13:05 on 16 Nov.

**18 Nov.** Optimizely's status page (14:49) states less than 5% of its customers were impacted, that no other Optimizely product was affected, and that every Web Experimentation customer was contacted.

**Scale and sites.** Report URI checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets it could find and found 188 infected, belonging to 178 organisations, and says the true number is likely higher. Its list includes (by its sector table) 32 banking/finance, 23 technology, 20 retail, 12 streaming, 10 news/media, 9 airlines/travel and 7 telecoms organisations. Named examples: Zoom, BBC (incl. BBC Earth and Top Gear), CNN, Fox News, NPR, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC (11 markets), Equifax (incl. Equifax UK), Air France-KLM/KLM, Ledger, Peacock, Alaska Airlines. UK-facing names on the list include Virgin Media, Virgin Media O2, O2, TalkTalk, ASOS, Admiral, Funding Circle, interactive investor, IG, tombola, Betfred, Freshfields and Baringa. Optimizely's own sites also carried the code. Helme told Newsweek the code may have loaded on roughly 34 million page visits (range 6–150 million), and stressed this counts loads, not victims.

**Duration.** For most sites the window was roughly 04:21/07:51 to about 21:00–22:24 on 16 Nov, i.e. StepSecurity says about 16 hours and IBTimes UK says the BBC copy was infected for nearly 17 hours (04:21 to 21:07). Optimizely's stated exposure window is 07:51–22:24 and per-customer windows are being given to customers directly.

**Company responses reported.** Salesforce said it disabled Optimizely scripts in preview and production; Equifax said it stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence of compromise of its systems; HSBC told Reuters/AFP unauthorised scripts were not active on its sites (iTnews understands HSBC disabled Optimizely globally, HSBC declined to comment on the record); TPG Telecom (Vodafone Australia) paused Optimizely and said affected pages had no payment or credential functions; IKEA said it was investigating. Reuters (via Dawn) said Apple, Zoom and CNN did not immediately comment. IBTimes UK found no public BBC statement as of Wednesday.
sections.technical:
**Vector (Optimizely's account, customer incident report 17 Nov).** A flaw in the Web Experimentation account signup flow let accounts created by the attacker act as existing administrator users on customer accounts, "through a combination of public information and brute force". Optimizely says the attacker guessed employee email-address variations, up to thousands of times per targeted customer, using Account/Project IDs that are visible in the public snippet; no customer passwords were stolen or used, no Optimizely admin account was compromised, and access to one customer did not give access to another. Attacker IPs included commercial VPN (ExpressVPN) addresses. The attacker then edited the Project JavaScript (`projectJS`) field of targeted projects (replacing any existing custom code). Optimizely's CDN served the modified file unchanged; Report URI states this was not CDN cache poisoning. No CVE has been assigned or published. Optimizely says the root cause and final IOC list will follow the Mandiant investigation.

**Payload (Report URI, StepSecurity, Socket analyses).** Loader variants: plain `<script>` to `https://1688360[.]cc/track.js`; the same URL base64-encoded via `atob()`; and a full inline copy run via `eval`. `track.js` was rebuilt 26 times on 16 Nov. Modules: (1) crypto address swapper (BTC, ETH/EVM, TRON, Solana, TON, LTC, BCH, DOGE) acting on page text, forms, clipboard, fetch/XHR; (2) card skimmer added 13:43, capturing Luhn-valid card number, expiry and CVV from the site's own forms/requests and sending to `/card.php` (hosted payment iframes such as Stripe/Adyen out of reach); (3) cookie (non-HttpOnly), URL and html2canvas screenshot exfiltration to `/hit.php` after an address swap; (4) iOS branch loading `boot.js` from `.icu` hosts and, per Report URI, the Coruna (iOS 13–17) and DarkSword (iOS 18.x) exploit kits plus an iOS 26 chain that only fingerprinted devices. Report URI says the kit's own comments list iOS 18.7.3+ and 26.3+ as patched. Report URI also reports the Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample from another campaign. Neither Report URI nor StepSecurity has evidence that any device was successfully compromised (public scans show exploit pages delivered, not success).

**Optimizely's description of the payload** differs in emphasis (see differing): it describes a skimmer loaded from `pay.pay-cloud[.]online` with exfiltration to `pay-relay.wordpressadmin001.workers[.]dev`, a 50 ms polling loop, mutation observers and clipboard listeners, and an iOS second stage targeting iOS/iPadOS 18.6 and lower.

**Published IOCs (defanged as published).** Report URI/Socket/StepSecurity: `1688360[.]cc` (`/track.js`, `/card.php`, `/hit.php`), `webshell[.]lol` (earlier injector), `5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu` and `eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu` (iOS loaders `/boot.js`), further `.icu` hosts listed by StepSecurity; page marker `window._k7`; Socket sample SHA-256 `1ec4245b3b303304ea24a89b3b2351b0f0c085087050f517d23dcba9694c165a` (one build only; StepSecurity notes other builds hash differently). Optimizely (preliminary, Mandiant): `pay-cloud[.]online`, `pay.pay-cloud[.]online`, `pay-relay.wordpressadmin001.workers[.]dev`. Optimizely lists two ExpressVPN IPs but says VPN IPs are not reliable IOCs. Wallet addresses are published by Report URI and not reproduced here.

**ATT&CK (analyst mapping; not published by Optimizely or the researchers).** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1189 Drive-by Compromise (iOS exploit delivery); T1059.007 JavaScript; T1115 Clipboard Data; T1113 Screen Capture; T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie.

**Attribution.** None. Optimizely says the actor is unnamed and attribution is pending; its preliminary research says the actor controls `pay-cloud[.]online`, has run two C2 frameworks (named ADAPTAGENT and CUPCAKE C2) from it since at least September, and that the same infrastructure hosts card skimmers used against other victims. Report URI links a TRON wallet in use since March 2026 and `webshell.lol` activity since 17 Sep to the same actor.

**Wider campaign (Hudson Rock, as relayed by Risky Business, Help Net Security, StepSecurity, iTWire).** Poisoned scripts from Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly (Risky Business and Report URI write "Minute Media") were observed from 13 Nov for Kissmetrics and StorifyMe and on 16 Nov for minute-ly (StepSecurity), and tied to the same iOS-routing infrastructure. Hudson Rock and researcher Kirk say the findings do not establish four independent vendor breaches or a single operator (relayed by Help Net Security and StepSecurity); StepSecurity says it has not verified the link between the webshell.lol injector and the same actor, or checked the archives itself. StorifyMe told iTWire unauthorised JavaScript reached some customer integrations, it removed the code, disabled custom JavaScript in widgets, rotated credentials and engaged external specialists. Newsweek reports Netskope research suggesting the wider malware campaign began in September (Netskope source not read).
sections.guidance: Published by Optimizely (incident report, 17 Nov; status page): the vulnerability was closed 16 Nov at 16:10 UTC and injected code removed from all affected projects by 22:24 UTC. Only Web Experimentation was affected; Feature Experimentation, the SDKs and legacy Full Stack were not. Optimizely says customers do not need to reset passwords or regenerate API tokens, that re-enabling the Web Experimentation snippet is now safe (its early 16 Nov advice to disable it was withdrawn), and lists recommended customer actions: review pages carrying the snippet during 07:51–22:24 UTC on 16 Nov, review CSP reports and outbound requests for the IOC domains, review card and crypto transactions in the window, retain logs, assess legal notification duties, check for a strong CSP, and remove the snippet from sensitive payment/crypto pages where no experiments run. Optimizely says a strong Content Security Policy blocked the injected script and hosted payment iframes were out of reach. Customers unaffected were told so individually; others can obtain per-site windows via their Customer Success Manager.
sections.differing:
**Start of malicious activity.** Optimizely: first malicious code written 07:51 UTC 16 Nov (first attacker account 00:37). Report URI: first injected Optimizely snippet seen at 04:21 UTC (BBC snippet loading `webshell.lol`). The ~3.5-hour gap is unreconciled; Optimizely's report calls its timeline preliminary and Mandiant's investigation is ongoing. Socket separately notes a Wayback capture of `track.js` at 08:08:15 UTC, before the 08:10 first-build time in Report URI's timeline, and says the relationship to the 26 builds is unconfirmed.

**End of exposure.** Optimizely: code removed from all affected projects by 22:24 UTC; delivery blocked at Cloudflare from 16:06. Report URI observed 186 of 1,611 snippets still infected at 19:24–19:59, mass clean-up 20:40–21:10 and one snippet infected at 21:52, with all clean by 23:11. StepSecurity found scan records of requests to the payload host until 21:23 UTC. iTnews converted both timelines to AEDT: Report URI's first injection at 3:21pm and mass clean-up by about 8:10am Tuesday (about 21:10 UTC on 16 Nov), and Optimizely's first malicious code at 6:51pm and removal from all affected projects by 9:24am Tuesday (22:24 UTC). Report URI also says Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned and then re-infected, which it reads as the attacker retaining access at that moment; Optimizely's report states the flaw was closed at 16:10 and does not address this.

**Payload scope and indicators.** Optimizely says its analysis found the script was intended to obtain payment information and crypto activity only, with data sent to the `workers[.]dev` endpoint, and that no personal data exfiltration is evidenced (it can see only when code loaded, not what was captured). Report URI, StepSecurity and Socket document a broader multi-module kit (clipper, skimmer, cookies/screenshots, iOS exploit kits) and `1688360[.]cc` infrastructure. Optimizely's own report also mentions cookie/screenshot capture and an iOS exploit attempt, but its published IOCs (`pay-cloud[.]online`, `workers[.]dev`) do not overlap with the researchers' (`1688360[.]cc`, `.icu`). Whether these are different payload versions, different stages, or different pieces of the same toolset has not been explained publicly.

**Mechanism.** Report URI (16 Nov) said it did not know how the attacker obtained write access to many unrelated customer projects and named possibilities (compromised Optimizely system, credential with cross-customer access, other). Optimizely's later report attributes it to the signup-flow flaw plus guessing of staff email addresses, per customer. StepSecurity noted Optimizely had not explained how a signup flaw gave write access across unrelated projects; Optimizely's report says each customer was targeted separately.

**Scale.** Report URI: 188 of 1,611 snippets (178 organisations), likely an undercount. Optimizely: less than 5% of customers impacted. These are not directly comparable (Report URI's sample is of snippets it could find, not a random sample).

**Money taken.** Report URI: about $7,040 received by attacker wallets by 19:25 UTC (Krebs cites about $7,500). StepSecurity repeats Report URI's $7,040 figure and cites Galaxy Digital's Alex Thorn estimating that victims sent about $2,300, with much of the Bitcoin appearing to be the attacker's own funds (StepSecurity could not confirm); Help Net Security gives about $7,150. Card and cookie theft cannot be seen on-chain; nobody has published a number.

**AI involvement.** Optimizely's status page says attackers are increasingly using AI and that it is responding; it does not state AI was used here. Helme told Newsweek researchers saw "no evidence of AI involvement"; ZeroFox's Peter Lowe told Newsweek he would not be surprised if it were an example of AI-assisted attack (speculation).

**Reporting discrepancies.** Il Sole 24 Ore (English edition, AI-translated) says the script was neutralised "within a few hours"; Optimizely's and Report URI's timelines show roughly 14–19 hours. Dawn/AFP say "nearly 200" sites and name HSBC UAE; Report URI's count is 178 organisations/188 snippets with HSBC in 11 markets.
sections.unknown:
Root-cause detail beyond Optimizely's summary; Mandiant's findings and final IOC list (Optimizely says the report may be delayed); the reconciled start time (04:21 vs 07:51 UTC) and actual per-site windows; how many cards, cookies or screenshots were exfiltrated (no one has published a number; Optimizely and Report URI both say they cannot see this); whether any iPhone/iPad was actually compromised by Coruna or DarkSword; number of visitors affected (Helme's ~34M page loads is an estimate of loads only); actor identity and whether the earlier Kissmetrics/StorifyMe/minute-ly and `webshell.lol` activity is one operator or the same compromise; whether the sites beyond Report URI's 1,611-snippet sample were affected; any regulator or breach-notification outcomes for affected organisations (none found; BBC had no public statement found).

**Label basis:** Optimizely itself confirmed the exploit, timeline and remediation (status page, customer incident report dated 17 Nov, statements to media); the malicious code and affected sites were independently documented by Report URI, StepSecurity, Socket and Hudson Rock, and several affected companies commented.

items.headline: Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI package compromised: versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 carried credential-stealing startup hooks
items.summary: Two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package were published to PyPI on 17 Nov 2026 and quarantined; they ran a credential stealer on every Python start and sent harvested secrets to a webhook.site endpoint.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened: 17 Nov 2026 (UTC): versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of agent-framework were published to PyPI, 33 minutes apart according to The Hacker News. The Hacker News gives an exposure window of roughly 20:35 to 21:20 UK time (stated as 8:35 to about 9:20 p.m. UTC). PyPI quarantined 1.26.1; BleepingComputer reports the second version was uploaded about 2.5 minutes later and quarantined about eight minutes after that. Researchers reported it on 17-18 Nov. BleepingComputer (18 Nov, 16:58 UK; 11:58 ET) and The Register (18 Nov 17:23 UK, updated 18:05 UK after a Microsoft comment) reported it on 18 Nov. Microsoft's spokesperson told The Register: "We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content." The agent-framework GitHub repository was offline when The Register wrote, per the report. ITmedia (19 Nov, 14:58 JST, translated from Japanese) reported both versions had been removed. The package is reported at about 190,000-200,000 monthly PyPI downloads.
sections.technical:
Both versions add a .pth file to site-packages, which Python executes on every interpreter start, whether or not agent_framework is imported. The legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0 is still installed as a dependency, so the framework works normally.

Version 1.26.1 (per Socket): agent_framework_meta.pth imports agent_framework_meta, whose __init__ starts agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py; that forks a detached process on Unix or uses a daemon thread elsewhere.

Version 1.26.2 (per Socket): af_runtime_diag.pth imports a top-level af_runtime_diag.py; the package __init__ is restored byte-for-byte, and GitHub Actions OIDC token requests are added.

Both collect environment variables matching credential patterns, credential files (Azure CLI, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config, Hugging Face, Azure DevOps agent files, .env and JSON files), Azure DevOps OIDC and managed-identity tokens, and Azure instance metadata; per Socket, the environment-variable selectors include AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI and HF_ in both versions, and BleepingComputer lists AWS, OpenAI and other services among the targets of 1.26.1. Data is JSON, zlib-compressed, base64-encoded and POSTed to a webhook.site endpoint hard-coded in the package (endpoint identifier withheld here; published by Socket). None of the sources read cites a CVE. Socket notes there is no persistent on-disk execution marker, so fresh process trees can trigger collection again; The Register describes the malware as running only while the malicious version remains in site-packages. Attack technique as described by researchers: supply-chain compromise of a published package, with startup-hook execution (the ATT&CK mapping is not published in the sources read).
sections.guidance: PyPI quarantined both versions (as reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News). Microsoft's spokesperson told The Register it had made some repositories private while investigating malicious content. The GitHub Advisory Database entry, as quoted by ITmedia, says credentials accessible from an environment with an affected version installed are to be treated as exposed. No Microsoft customer guidance was found.
sections.differing: Microsoft (spokesperson, via The Register): repositories made private while malicious content is investigated; "Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem." It has not said how publishing access was obtained. BleepingComputer says it asked Microsoft for the point of breach and got no reply by its publication time. The Register's own assessment is that the incident "appears" to involve unauthorised access to an administrator account on Microsoft's GitHub organisation; it names no source for this, and no confirmation from Microsoft or the researchers cited was found in the sources reviewed. OX Security, as cited by The Register, says the second upload was made through Microsoft's official PyPI publisher account. ITmedia cites StepSecurity saying a new maintainer account was created and added to the project on the same day; the StepSecurity post itself was not read.
sections.unknown:
How the attacker obtained PyPI publishing access; whether GitHub org admin credentials were compromised as The Register suggests; whether the ONNX Runtime repository going offline is related (The Register says neither Microsoft nor researchers have linked it); scope of affected environments and the number of installs; whether the webhook.site endpoint received data (none of the sources reviewed reports receipts); whether other Microsoft PyPI projects are affected (The Hacker News calls this the second Microsoft-related PyPI package compromised this year, after durabletask in May 2026, which it attributes to TeamPCP).

**Label basis:** Malicious code analysed in body text by Socket (primary research post), with matching technical accounts in The Hacker News, BleepingComputer, The Register and ITmedia; PyPI quarantine of both versions is reported by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and ITmedia (citing StepSecurity). Microsoft has confirmed only that it made repositories private while investigating; it has not described the compromise. Root cause is unconfirmed.

items.headline: Ruby patches 'Ruby2Shell' (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5), a one-byte heap overflow that Veria Labs says gives unauthenticated RCE in default Rails apps, alongside six other regex/string flaws
items.summary: Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10 (released 18 Nov) fix seven memory-safety flaws; maintainers rate the case-conversion bug Critical and know of RCE PoCs; the Ruby advisory shows no CVE yet (Aikido cites CVE-2026-132825), THN and Aikido report no attacks, and researchers plan a public PoC in about a week.
items.label: CONFIRMED

sections.happened:
**23 Oct 2026:** Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 released with fixes for earlier regular-expression compilation bugs found by GitLab (per The Hacker News; a different set of bugs). The same day, researcher Moritz Sanft (Durendal) says he began auditing Ruby's pre-authentication attack surface (his own account).

**5–7 Nov:** per Sanft's timeline, OpenAI sent the Ruby security team reports and then working exploit proofs for two bugs (the sharp-s overflow and a case-mapping integer overflow). This is the researcher's account; the Ruby advisory credits different reporters (see Differing accounts).

**18 Nov:** Ruby published the security announcement (posted by mame) and released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. The advisory page history stamps original publication at 19 Nov 00:00 UTC (00:00 UK); the GitHub advisory is dated 19 Nov.

**19 Nov:** Veria Labs published the 'ruby2ßhell' write-up with an affected-software table (page last updated 11:30 UTC). Durendal's write-up is dated 19 Nov. The Hacker News published at 08:42 UK. Aikido Security published its advisory (page modified 11:29 UTC).

**Current status (about 11:35 UK, 19 Nov):** Ruby's advisory and GitHub entry still show no CVE (requested); Veria's page says 'CVE pending'; Aikido's page now titles the flaw CVE-2026-132825, which Ruby has not confirmed. The Hacker News (describing the advisories) and Aikido report no attacks so far; Ruby's announcement does not address exploitation. Veria says it will publish a PoC 'in a week'.

The Ruby announcement covers seven flaws. The Hacker News reports the project's ratings as three critical, three high and one moderate, with RCE PoCs for five.
sections.technical:
**Ruby2Shell = GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5** (CWE-193 off-by-one per GitHub advisory; rated Critical by Ruby). No CVE on Ruby's advisory (requested); Aikido cites CVE-2026-132825. No CVSS published.

**Root cause (Veria Labs, Durendal):** in several single-byte encodings (ISO-8859-x, Windows-125x) the case-mapping loop checks for room for only one output byte, but upcasing ß (0xDF) emits two bytes ('SS'). The output buffer is input length + 20 bytes, so 21 ß characters overflow it by one byte (0x53 when upcasing, 0x73 when case-folding). Reached via `upcase`, `swapcase`, `downcase(:fold)`, `casecmp?` and the Symbol equivalents. Present since Ruby 2.4.0. UTF-8 takes a different path and is not affected. Veria also reports a one-byte out-of-bounds read when copying the result. Upstream fix: ruby/ruby commit d582f8f (per Veria).

**Reachability in Rails (Durendal's account):** Rack's `_method` override calls `.upcase` on a multipart field, and Rack lets the client set the field charset, so a multipart `_method` field with `charset=ISO-8859-1` containing ß characters reaches the bug. Veria lists Rails and classic-style Sinatra as affected by default, and plain Rack and other frameworks as not exposed by default. The ATT&CK mapping is the brief's, not published by the sources: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application).

**Affected (Ruby advisory):** 3.3.13 and earlier; 3.4.0–3.4.12; 4.0.0–4.0.9. Fixed in 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end-of-life and 'will not receive these fixes' (Ruby); Veria and Aikido say affected back to 2.4.0.

**Other six advisories (all pending CVEs):** GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x (regex double free, `&&` character class; critical; RCE PoC), GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w (regex compilation heap overflow; critical; RCE PoC), GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px (case-conversion integer overflow, >4 GiB result; high; RCE PoC; Durendal says Rack 3.2.2 and later limit multipart sizes that block the request), GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 (Regexp#to_s overflow; high; RCE PoC), GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r (case-insensitive match out-of-bounds read; high; PoC shows controlled memory corruption), GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h (case-insensitive backreference read; moderate; disclosure or crash). Ratings and PoC details per The Hacker News summary of the per-advisory pages. The regex flaws require an application that compiles attacker-controlled patterns, except GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h.

**Bundled Ruby in self-hosted products (Veria table, updated 19 Nov 11:30 UTC):** GitLab 19.6.0 (Ruby 3.3.13) affected; GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 (4.0.9) affected; Chatwoot 4.20.0 (3.4.4) affected; Mastodon 4.7.6, OpenProject 17.9.8 and the Discourse base image 2.0.20261119-0203 now on Ruby 4.0.10 and marked fixed. Aikido's table lists Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7 and Discourse 2026.10.1 as affected (different release numbers from Veria's).

**IOCs / signatures:** none published in the Ruby, Veria, Durendal or Aikido pages.
sections.guidance:
**Ruby maintainers:** 'strongly recommend upgrading' to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Ruby 3.3 moved from security maintenance to legacy maintenance with 3.3.14, with support still scheduled to end at the end of March 2027. The GitHub advisory says to upgrade to the same versions, and the maintainers have requested CVE IDs.

No advisory from GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server or Chatwoot was found in the sources reviewed.

Durendal says OpenAI coordinated with WAF providers around the release. No WAF vendor statement was found.
sections.differing:
**Reporter credit:** the Ruby advisory credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic for GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, and 'baba__yaga' for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px. Durendal's author says he found both bugs on 23 Oct using Codex and that OpenAI reported them to Ruby. Veria Labs published the named write-up and affected-product table. The sources read do not reconcile these accounts; they may reflect independent discovery. The Ruby project's credit is the official record.

**Scope of exposure:** the Ruby advisory says RCE PoCs exist 'in some scenarios'. Veria says default Rails and classic Sinatra are reachable without authentication. Durendal says it was exploited against a plain `rails new` app with jemalloc and the default glibc allocator, and that it 'should' work on 'many' apps including GitHub and GitLab. These are researcher claims; the PoCs are not public and were not independently verified.

**Affected-product status:** Veria's table (updated 11:30 UTC) marks Mastodon 4.7.6, OpenProject 17.9.8 and the Discourse base image 2.0.20261119-0203 as fixed on Ruby 4.0.10, while Aikido's table (modified 11:29 UTC) lists Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7 and Discourse 2026.10.1 as affected. The two tables cite different release numbers, so they are not directly contradictory; no vendor release notes were reviewed.

**CVE assignment:** Ruby's announcement and GitHub advisory say CVE IDs have been requested and show none; Veria's page says 'CVE pending'. Aikido's page titles the flaw CVE-2026-132825 and no other source reviewed confirms it.
sections.unknown:
- Official CVE IDs and CVSS scores (requested; Aikido's CVE-2026-132825 is not confirmed by Ruby).
- Whether exploitation has begun. The Hacker News (describing the advisories) and Aikido report none; Ruby's announcement is silent.
- Public PoC: Veria says about a week after disclosure.
- Fix timing for GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server and Chatwoot; no vendor statements were found.
- Whether other frameworks or application code expose the legacy-encoding path, and how many internet-facing Rails apps process such input.
- Reconciliation of reporter credits (Anthropic/Ada Logics vs OpenAI/Durendal).

**Label basis:** The Ruby project's own security advisory and GitHub repository advisory confirm the flaws, severity, affected/fixed versions and existence of RCE PoCs; the 'unauthenticated, default Rails' reachability rests on Veria Labs and a second researcher, not on the maintainers.
